stem: Pt present 5 day after op with foul smelling greenish discharge from surgical wound What's the responsible organism?
why_right: The decisive clue is greenish discharge. Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces blue-green pigments (pyocyanin) and a distinctive odor, so a green, foul-smelling wound discharge points to it. It is a classic pathogen in burns and in moist, hospital-acquired wound infections.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staph aureus is the most common surgical site infection organism overall, but it gives thick creamy-yellow pus, not green discharge.
B. Strep pyogenes causes spreading cellulitis and lymphangitis, often early, with thin serous discharge rather than green pus.
C. Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene: severe pain, crepitus, gas in the tissues and dark "dishwater" discharge after contaminated wounds, not green pus.
key_concept:
Wound discharge color/character points to the organism.
  • Green/blue-green, sweet or foul odor: Pseudomonas
  • Creamy yellow pus: Staph aureus (most common SSI)
  • Rapid spreading cellulitis, red streaks: Strep pyogenes
  • Crepitus, gas, myonecrosis: Clostridium perfringens
  • Prosthetic/graft infection: Staph epidermidis
exam_pearl: "Most common SSI organism" = Staph aureus, but if the stem says green, the answer is Pseudomonas.

stem: male patient presented to the clinic worried regarding the possibility of melanoma, given a family history of melanoma (his father)The patient has multiple benign nevi
why_right: A patient with "multiple" nevi plus a first-degree relative (his father) with melanoma has two major melanoma risk factors. He should be referred to a dermatologist for a full skin examination, baseline mapping and regular surveillance, and taught self-examination and sun protection.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance alone ignores his raised risk; it fits a low-risk patient with few typical nevi and no family history.
key_concept:
Melanoma risk: many nevi (or atypical nevi), family history, fair skin, sunburn history, immunosuppression, previous melanoma.
  • High risk → dermatology surveillance (full skin exam, ± photography or dermoscopy)
  • Suspicious lesion (ABCDE change) → excisional biopsy with narrow margins
  • Education: sun protection and monthly self-examination
exam_pearl: A changing or ABCDE-positive mole changes the answer from referral for surveillance to excisional biopsy.

stem: A colic baby with leg raise and crying ( there was no swaddling or white noise )
why_right: Crying episodes with leg raising in an otherwise well infant describe infantile colic, a benign, self-limited condition that usually settles by around 3 to 4 months. Management is supportive: reassure the parents and teach soothing strategies. With swaddling and white noise not offered, reassurance is the remaining correct supportive option.
why_wrong_block: B. Herbal teas have no proven benefit for colic and may displace milk feeds in a young infant; they are not recommended.
key_concept:
Infantile colic (rule of 3s): crying more than 3 hours/day, more than 3 days/week, for more than 3 weeks in a healthy infant.
  • Typical in the first 3 months of life
  • Management: reassurance plus behavioural soothing (holding, rocking, swaddling, white noise)
  • No medication or routine formula change
  • Red flags (fever, vomiting, poor weight gain, blood in stool) need workup
exam_pearl: Well, thriving infant with paroxysmal crying and drawn-up legs = colic: reassure, do not medicate.

stem: Mother of a 2-month-old infant complains that her baby has frequent episodes of excessive crying for 3 hours, raises legs and passes gas. What is the appropriate management?
OptB: Swaddling and use of white noise
why_right: A 2-month-old with excessive crying for "3 hours", leg raising and gas, with no red flags, has infantile colic. Treatment is reassurance and behavioural soothing, and swaddling with white noise is a recommended soothing technique. It is the only option that is safe and recommended for this benign, self-limited condition.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simethicone has no proven benefit over placebo for colic, despite the "passes gas" clue; medication is not recommended.
C. There is no fever or sign of infection; antibiotics have no role in colic.
D. Imaging is for red flags such as bilious vomiting, a mass, fever or poor growth (for example intussusception); a well infant with typical colic needs no investigation.
key_concept:
Colic = diagnosis of a well, thriving infant; management is non-pharmacological.
  • Rule of 3s: more than 3 h/day, more than 3 days/week, more than 3 weeks
  • Peaks in the first 3 months
  • Soothing: holding, rocking, swaddling, white noise, parental support
  • Avoid: simethicone, colic drops, routine formula change
  • Episodic crying with vomiting, lethargy or mass in an older infant = think intussusception
exam_pearl: "Passes gas" tempts you to simethicone; colic is treated with soothing and reassurance, not drops.

stem: 6 years old boy came to clinic with , pale and Ecchymosis and petechiae post upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago ،boy now is well demarcated of bruising and petechiae . ( lab platelets was low cant remember the exact number) what is most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Low Platelets Normal Hb Normal WBC
highlight_terms_source: post upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago
Low Platelets Normal Hb Normal WBC
why_right: Petechiae and bruising 2 weeks after a URTI in a well 6-year-old with isolated thrombocytopenia (normal Hb, normal WBC) is acute childhood ITP. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the peripheral blood smear confirms it by showing true thrombocytopenia (excluding clumping) with large platelets and no blasts, schistocytes or other abnormal cells. A typical picture plus a normal smear is enough to make the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulation factors (PT, aPTT) are normal in ITP; they are right when bleeding suggests a factor problem such as hemophilia (joint or deep bleeding, prolonged aPTT) or DIC.
B. Bone marrow examination is reserved for atypical features, such as abnormal Hb or WBC, blasts, organomegaly, bone pain or failure to respond, where leukemia or marrow failure must be excluded.
D. Antiplatelet antibody testing has poor sensitivity and specificity and is not used to diagnose ITP.
key_concept:
Childhood ITP: isolated low platelets after a viral illness in a well child.
  • Typical age 2 to 6 years, usually acute and self-limited
  • Confirm: CBC plus peripheral smear (large platelets, otherwise normal)
  • Marrow if done: normal or increased megakaryocytes
  • Bone marrow only if atypical (cytopenias in other lines, organomegaly, bone pain)
  • Management: observation if only skin bleeding; IVIG or steroids if severe; platelets only for life-threatening bleeding
exam_pearl: Low platelets with normal Hb and WBC = smear; add anemia, high WBC or bone pain = bone marrow for leukemia.

stem: Child with high fever sore throat and mild erythematous rash O/E multiple mosquito bites, how to manage: Vitals are stable except for fever of 39
highlight_terms_source: high fever sore throat and mild erythematous rash
why_right: High fever, myalgia, a mild erythematous rash, multiple mosquito bites and borderline platelets suggest a viral infection, most likely dengue in a mosquito-endemic setting. With "stable vitals" and no warning signs, management is supportive: oral hydration and paracetamol for fever, with monitoring for warning signs. Fluids are the cornerstone because plasma leakage is the main danger.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs are avoided in suspected dengue because they worsen bleeding risk with falling platelets; paracetamol is the antipyretic of choice.
B. The picture is viral and the child is stable; empiric antibiotics are indicated only for suspected bacterial sepsis or an unstable, toxic child.
key_concept:
Suspected dengue (fever, myalgia, rash, mosquito exposure, low or falling platelets):
  • No warning signs: oral fluids, paracetamol, rest, close follow-up
  • Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin (bleeding risk)
  • Warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, rising hematocrit with falling platelets: admit for IV fluids
  • No role for antibiotics or steroids
exam_pearl: Fever with mosquito bites and low platelets: paracetamol plus fluids, never ibuprofen.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot of same recall adds: patient had severe myalgia and labs showed normal Hb and platelets of 130? 170? (platelets borderline low, recaller not sure, did not think below 150); screenshot shows option A- Ibuprofen for fever only.

stem: Which of the following viral gastroenteritis can be prevented by vaccination?
why_right: Rotavirus is the only listed cause of viral gastroenteritis with a licensed vaccine. It is an oral live attenuated vaccine given in infancy and is part of the Saudi routine schedule starting at 2 months, which has greatly reduced severe dehydrating diarrhea in young children.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adenovirus (enteric types) causes childhood gastroenteritis, but there is no licensed vaccine for adenoviral gastroenteritis.
B. Astrovirus causes mild gastroenteritis in young children; no vaccine is licensed.
C. Norovirus is the leading cause of outbreak gastroenteritis across all ages, but no vaccine is licensed yet.
key_concept:
Viral gastroenteritis causes and prevention:
  • Rotavirus: severe watery diarrhea in infants; oral vaccine in the routine schedule from 2 months
  • Norovirus: outbreaks (cruise ships, schools), all ages; hygiene only
  • Adenovirus and astrovirus: milder pediatric disease; no vaccine
  • Diagnosis when needed: stool antigen (ELISA)
exam_pearl: Only rotavirus gastroenteritis is vaccine preventable; norovirus is the common distractor.

stem: 7 year old boy his father has TB , he has PPD of 14 mm , CXR is negative , what is the next step?
why_right: The child is a household contact ("father has TB"), a group in which a TST of 5 mm or more is already positive, so 14 mm is clearly positive. With a negative CXR (and no stated symptoms) active disease is excluded, which makes this latent TB infection. The next step is to treat it (chemoprophylaxis, for example isoniazid or a rifampicin based regimen) to prevent progression to active TB.
why_wrong_block: B. IGRA is an alternative screening test (useful when BCG makes a TST hard to interpret), not a confirmatory step after a clearly positive TST in a close contact; repeating testing only delays treatment.
key_concept:
Positive TST + normal CXR + no symptoms = latent TB: treat it.
  • ≥5 mm positive: recent contact of active TB, HIV, immunosuppressed, fibrotic CXR
  • ≥10 mm positive: children under 4, high risk settings, migrants from endemic areas
  • ≥15 mm positive: no risk factors
  • Abnormal CXR or symptoms: work up for active TB (sputum or gastric aspirate) and give full therapy instead
  • LTBI options: isoniazid 6 months, rifampicin 4 months, or isoniazid + rifampicin 3 months
exam_pearl: Cutoff depends on risk group: a contact with ≥5 mm is positive; an abnormal CXR switches you from prophylaxis to active TB workup.

stem: Patient with trauma to the thigh about 4cm with visible underline tissues and bone. What is the initial treatment?
OptC: IV antibiotics within the first hour
why_right: This recall's key is a compressive dressing because the very first hands-on step for a large open thigh wound ("4 cm", "visible underlying tissues and bone") is to cover it and control bleeding with direct pressure before anything else is arranged. A sterile, moist pressure dressing stops ongoing blood loss, limits further contamination and is done at the bedside within minutes, while the rest of the open fracture pathway (antibiotics, tetanus, debridement, fixation) follows.
why_wrong_block:
B. Analgesia and fluids are supportive and are given alongside, but they do not address the open wound itself; fluids become the priority only if the patient is in shock.
C. Early IV antibiotics are essential in every open fracture and are started in the ED, but in this recall's logic they follow covering and controlling the wound; they would be the answer if the stem stressed that bleeding is controlled and asked about infection prevention.
D. Debridement and stabilization are the definitive treatment done in theatre after initial ED care (dressing, antibiotics, tetanus, splinting); they are not the initial step.
key_concept:
Open fracture pathway: control bleeding and cover the wound, then IV antibiotics and tetanus, then debridement and irrigation, then fixation.
  • External bleeding: direct pressure first; tourniquet only if pressure fails.
  • Bone visible through a wound = open fracture.
  • IV antibiotics and tetanus are started in the ED, before surgery.
  • Debridement plus irrigation in theatre, then definitive fixation (IM nail for long bones).
  • Splint/realign the limb and recheck distal pulses.
exam_pearl: "Initial" = what you do with your hands at the bedside now; "definitive" = debridement and fixation in theatre.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0379 → C. IV antibiotics within the first hour. Confirm before the exam.

stem: 11 yo female with signs and symptoms of SLE and anti-dsna positive With low complements She is on mtx already What to add
why_right: Hydroxychloroquine is the cornerstone of therapy for every SLE patient unless contraindicated, and it reduces flares and organ damage. This child has active serology (anti-dsDNA positive, low complements) and is on methotrexate alone, with no renal or CNS disease described, so the missing backbone drug is hydroxychloroquine (HCQ + MTX is the standard mild to moderate combination).
why_wrong_block:
A. Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe organ threatening lupus, classically neuropsychiatric lupus or severe nephritis; no such involvement is described.
C. MMF is the preferred immunosuppressant for lupus nephritis; it would be right if proteinuria, active sediment or rising creatinine were given, not as the next add on here.
key_concept:
All SLE gets hydroxychloroquine; then match the add on to the organ.
  • Skin and joints: HCQ + methotrexate (± low dose steroid)
  • Kidney (lupus nephritis): MMF
  • CNS (neuropsychiatric lupus): cyclophosphamide
  • Life threatening disease: high dose steroid + immunosuppressant
  • Pregnancy: stop MMF, switch to azathioprine, continue HCQ
exam_pearl: If the patient is not on HCQ yet, adding HCQ beats escalating to a stronger immunosuppressant unless kidney or CNS involvement is stated.

stem: Patient 11 y with every symptom of active SLE malar rash and active arthritis but no cns on renal problems 100% sure the labs all are the classic labs ex c3 was low and creatinine normal but the patient is not on any drug and they did not say he was diagnosed before What is the management now?
why_right: This is a new, untreated SLE ("not on any drug") with skin and joint disease (malar rash, active arthritis) and no renal or CNS involvement (normal creatinine). That is mild to moderate lupus, and hydroxychloroquine is the cornerstone first line drug for every SLE patient; low C3 reflects activity but does not by itself demand cytotoxic therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Azathioprine is a steroid sparing or maintenance agent (and the pregnancy compatible substitute for MMF), not the first drug in new mucocutaneous and joint lupus.
C. Cyclophosphamide is for severe organ threatening disease, classically neuropsychiatric lupus; the stem explicitly says no CNS involvement.
D. MMF is the choice for lupus nephritis; it would fit if proteinuria or active urinary sediment were present, but renal function is normal here.
key_concept:
New SLE without kidney or CNS involvement: start hydroxychloroquine.
  • Mild to moderate (skin, joints): HCQ, then add methotrexate and low dose steroid if not controlled
  • Nephritis: MMF
  • Neuropsychiatric lupus: cyclophosphamide
  • Anti-dsDNA and low complement track activity, especially renal
exam_pearl: "No CNS, no renal" is the clue that removes cyclophosphamide and MMF; HCQ is the default.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Answer: B' printed at top of next page.

stem: A pediatric patient with white eye reflex. What to order to confirm diagnosis
why_right: A child with leukocoria is suspected of retinoblastoma. This recall's key is MRI because it is the imaging of choice to characterise the tumour and assess optic nerve, orbital and intracranial extension without exposing the child to radiation, which matters because hereditary RB1 carriers are at risk of radiation induced second cancers.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT shows calcification well but is avoided in suspected retinoblastoma because ionising radiation raises second cancer risk in RB1 carriers.
C. Ocular ultrasound (B scan) is the quick bedside test that demonstrates an intraocular mass with calcification; it is not the keyed answer here but is often used first.
D. Plain X ray has no role in evaluating an intraocular mass.
key_concept:
Leukocoria workup: urgent ophthalmology, dilated fundus exam under anaesthesia, then imaging without radiation.
  • Ultrasound B scan: confirms intraocular mass and calcification
  • MRI orbits and brain: extent, optic nerve invasion, pineal lesion
  • CT: avoided (radiation, second cancers in RB1 carriers)
  • Biopsy: not done (risk of tumour seeding)
exam_pearl: CT is the trap: it shows calcium best but is avoided in retinoblastoma because of radiation.

stem: 4 years old with night time enuresis , never been dry , his mother is worried , what is the most reasonable advice you can give? (Written like this)
OptD: I don’t recall but something wrong
why_right: Night time wetting in a 4 year old who has never been dry is primary nocturnal enuresis, and bladder control at night is not expected until about age 5. With no daytime symptoms, red flags or other complaints described, the most reasonable advice is reassurance that this is within normal development and usually resolves spontaneously (a urinalysis is a reasonable simple check).
why_wrong_block:
A. Urology referral is for red flags: daytime symptoms with recurrent UTI (renal US and VCUG), abnormal neurologic or spine findings, or a structural cause; none are described.
B. Behavioral therapy (alarm, reward charts) is used for persistent enuresis after about 5 to 6 years; at 4 years it is premature and can add stress.
D. This option was not recalled; whatever it was, active intervention or referral is not needed for monosymptomatic enuresis at this age.
key_concept:
Enuresis is diagnosed only from about age 5; below that, reassure.
  • Primary: never dry; secondary: wet again after a dry period (look for stress, UTI, diabetes)
  • Every child: urinalysis
  • Recurrent UTI: renal US + VCUG
  • Spine deformity or abnormal neuro exam: MRI spine
  • Persistent after 5 to 6 years: enuresis alarm first, desmopressin as alternative
exam_pearl: Age decides it: a 4 year old wetting at night is normal; a previously dry child who starts wetting is secondary and needs a cause.

stem: Preterm presents with nasal flaring and grunting. What is the appropriate management?
OptD: Insert 2 tubes in the bronchus (something similar)
why_right: A preterm infant with grunting and nasal flaring has respiratory distress syndrome until proven otherwise, caused by surfactant deficiency of the immature lung. The definitive treatment is exogenous surfactant given intratracheally (with respiratory support such as CPAP), which improves compliance and reduces mortality and air leak.
why_wrong_block:
B. Corticosteroids prevent RDS when given to the mother before preterm delivery; they are not the treatment for an infant already showing RDS.
C. Antibiotics are added when sepsis or congenital pneumonia is suspected (maternal fever, PROM, chorioamnionitis); they do not treat surfactant deficiency, which is the problem in an otherwise unremarkable preterm.
D. Chest tubes or bronchial intubation are for complications such as pneumothorax or for ventilation, not the specific management of RDS.
key_concept:
Preterm + grunting, flaring, retractions = RDS: CPAP and intratracheal surfactant.
  • RDS: preterm, ground glass CXR with air bronchograms
  • TTN: term, often C section, fluid in the fissure, resolves in 1 to 3 days
  • Meconium aspiration: post term, meconium stained liquor, patchy infiltrates
  • Prevention: antenatal steroids to the mother in threatened preterm labor
  • Maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturity, so RDS can occur nearer term
exam_pearl: Steroids prevent RDS (mother, before delivery); surfactant treats it (baby, after delivery).

stem: One new question about 6 month child came with his father to clinic c/o reducible pulge in center of his abdomen increase with crying
highlight_terms_source: reducible pulge in center of his abdomen
why_right: A reducible bulge at the center of the abdomen (umbilicus) that increases with crying in a well 6 month old is a classic umbilical hernia: a fascial defect through which skin covered contents protrude with raised intra-abdominal pressure. Most close spontaneously, so the usual plan is observation.
why_wrong_block: B. Omphalocele is a congenital midline defect present at birth, with bowel or liver covered by a membrane (amnion and peritoneum) and the cord inserting into the sac; it does not appear later as a skin covered bulge only on crying.
key_concept:
Skin covered, reducible umbilical bulge on crying = umbilical hernia: observe.
  • Most close spontaneously by about 2 to 4 years
  • Surgery: incarceration or strangulation, or persistence at about 4 years
  • Strapping or coins do not help
  • Omphalocele: membrane covered, at birth, associated anomalies
  • Gastroschisis: right of the cord, no sac, exposed bowel
exam_pearl: Skin covered and appearing later = hernia; membrane covered and present at birth = omphalocele.

stem: Patient diagnosed with acute pancreatitis 3 weeks ago, now present to ER Complain of mild abdominal pain and tenderness, showed cyst measure 4 cm. How you will manage?
key_concept:
Post-pancreatitis cyst: decide by size, age, symptoms and infection.
  • Under 6 cm, under 6 weeks, minimal symptoms: observe.
  • Over 6 cm, over 6 weeks, growing or symptomatic: endoscopic internal drainage.
  • Infected/abscess (fever, WBC up, gas): percutaneous drainage.
  • Surgery: failed endoscopic drainage or suspected neoplasm.
  • A collection under 4 weeks old is not yet a mature walled pseudocyst.
exam_pearl: Fever or leukocytosis flips any cyst answer to percutaneous drainage; no fever, small and young flips it to observation.

stem: Child glucose 38 Blood sample taken before correction not mention about mother hx Insulin fasting 40 was normal regarding refrence range was upto 110 ACTH 500 was slightly high What is the cause of
why_right: The key is the critical sample taken during hypoglycemia (glucose 38, "before correction"). During true hypoglycemia insulin should be fully suppressed, so an insulin value that is merely "normal" is inappropriately high and points to hyperinsulinism. The mildly raised ACTH fits the expected stress response to hypoglycemia rather than primary adrenal failure.
why_wrong_block: A. Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycemia with low cortisol and a suppressed insulin; it would be the answer if cortisol were low with a clearly high ACTH (often with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypotension), not with unsuppressed insulin.
key_concept:
Interpret every hormone against the glucose at that moment.
  • Hypoglycemia + detectable or "normal" insulin = hyperinsulinism
  • Hyperinsulinism also shows low ketones and low free fatty acids
  • Low cortisol + high ACTH = primary adrenal insufficiency
  • High ketones with appropriately suppressed insulin: ketotic hypoglycemia, hormone deficiency
  • Always draw the critical sample before giving glucose
exam_pearl: A "normal" insulin during hypoglycemia is abnormal; normal ranges apply only to normal glucose.

stem: 6 years old Patient with clear case of brucellosis. Hx of Drink raw milk patint had pain in the knee. Which if the following is the first line treatment ?
why_right: Brucellosis (raw milk, joint pain) in a 6 year old: the adult first line regimen is doxycycline based, but tetracyclines are avoided in children under 8 years because of tooth staining and bone effects. The pediatric first line is therefore TMP-SMX plus rifampicin for 6 weeks; a combination is needed because monotherapy relapses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks is first line for adults and children 8 years or older; at 6 years doxycycline is avoided.
C. Ciprofloxacin alone is monotherapy (high relapse rate) and quinolones are not first line in brucellosis, especially in children.
D. Ceftriaxone has poor intracellular activity against Brucella and is not a standard regimen; single agent therapy also relapses.
key_concept:
Brucellosis always needs combination therapy; age and pregnancy pick the partner.
  • Adults and children ≥8 years: doxycycline 6 weeks + rifampicin 6 weeks (or streptomycin for the first 2 to 3 weeks)
  • Children under 8: TMP-SMX + rifampicin for 6 weeks
  • Pregnancy: rifampicin based, avoid doxycycline
  • Spondylitis or sacroiliitis: about 12 weeks
  • Neurobrucellosis: about 6 months
exam_pearl: Same disease, different answer: the child's age under 8 removes doxycycline.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0947D).

stem: A 70y old male patient with prostate cancer undergoing robotic surgery. He is known case of hypertension and had a previous stroke. He is on anticoagulant which was stopped 5 days ago.Which of the following enhances safety of the surgery?
OptC: Check medication cessation and monitor bleeding
highlight_terms_source: on anticoagulant which was stopped 5 days ago
why_right: In a patient on anticoagulation ("stopped 5 days ago") with prior stroke going for major robotic prostatectomy, the safety step is to confirm the drug was actually stopped for the right interval (and coagulation is acceptable) and then watch closely for bleeding. This is part of the pre-op checklist (sign-in/time-out) and directly reduces the main perioperative risk: hemorrhage.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skipping the team briefing removes the checklist step that catches errors such as unchecked anticoagulation; briefing is never skipped.
B. Anesthetic dosing is titrated to the patient, never given "randomly"; underdosing risks awareness and hemodynamic instability.
D. Restarting anticoagulation right before surgery greatly raises bleeding risk; it is resumed after surgery once hemostasis is secure (with bridging decided case by case).
key_concept:
Peri-op anticoagulation safety: confirm cessation, check coagulation, plan when to restart.
  • Verify last dose and that the stopping interval was adequate.
  • Run the surgical safety checklist (sign-in, time-out, sign-out).
  • Anticipate and monitor blood loss intra- and post-op.
  • Restart anticoagulation after surgery when bleeding risk allows; bridging for high thrombotic risk.
exam_pearl: Stroke history tempts you to "protect" with anticoagulation, but pre-op the priority is bleeding control; restart after surgery.

stem: Name of the reflex? (images: infant held upright with feet touching surface, making stepping movements)
why_right: The images show the infant held upright with the feet touching a surface, making alternating step movements. This walking-like response is the stepping reflex, present at birth and normally fading in the first couple of months.
why_wrong_block: A. Rooting reflex: a mouth response, turning toward a touch on the cheek or corner of the mouth; it involves no leg movement.
key_concept:
Name the reflex from the stimulus:
  • Feet on surface, upright: stepping
  • Dorsum of foot touches table edge: placing
  • Cheek stroked: rooting
  • Head turned supine, fencing posture: ATNR
  • Head drop: Moro
  • Held face down toward table, arms extend: parachute (appears 8 to 10 months)
exam_pearl: Sole touching the surface gives stepping; the top of the foot touching an edge gives placing.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0348B).
Compiler note: Answer shown bold in screenshot.

stem: Time of disappearance? (stepping reflex)
why_right: The stepping (walking) reflex, alternate leg lifting when the infant is held upright with soles on a surface, is present at birth and is one of the earliest primitive reflexes to fade, usually by about 2 months.
why_wrong_block:
B. By 4 months is the disappearance age of the rooting and Galant (trunk incurvation) reflexes.
C. By 6 months is when the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes disappear.
key_concept:
Primitive reflex disappearance ages:
  • Stepping: about 2 months
  • ATNR (fencing): about 2 to 3 months
  • Rooting, Galant: about 4 months
  • Moro, palmar grasp: about 6 months
  • Babinski: 12 to 18 months
  • Parachute: appears 8 to 10 months and persists for life
exam_pearl: Persistence of primitive reflexes beyond their expected age suggests CNS pathology such as cerebral palsy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer shown bold in screenshot.

stem: 12 month old came with his mother, she’s worried about autim because his cousin has it, what advice will you give her?
why_right: Formal autism screening (for example M-CHAT) is done at the 18 and 24 month visits, and the child here is only 12 months. The mother's concern is reasonable given a family history, so the best advice explains that the child will be screened at 18 to 24 months (with ongoing developmental surveillance and earlier review if red flags appear), rather than simply dismissing her worry.
why_wrong_block: B. Plain reassurance ignores a real family history and gives no follow up plan; reassurance alone fits only when there is no risk factor and development is normal, and even then routine screening still happens at 18 to 24 months.
key_concept:
Autism: surveillance at every visit, formal screening at 18 and 24 months.
  • Red flags at 12 months: no babbling, no pointing or gestures, no response to name
  • No single words by 16 months or no 2 word phrases by 24 months
  • Any loss of language or social skills at any age
  • Red flag or positive screen: refer for full developmental evaluation and hearing test
  • Siblings of affected children have higher risk
exam_pearl: If red flags are already present, refer now; screening age is only the default for a child developing normally.

stem: Neonate with TTN and severe respiratory distress on mechanical ventilator but he is not improving, next step:
highlight_terms_source: on mechanical ventilator but he is not improving
key_concept:
TTN is usually mild and settles on its own; severe or worsening distress means escalate support and rethink the diagnosis.
  • TTN: term or near term, C-section, retained fetal lung fluid, perihilar streaks on CXR, self resolving
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground glass CXR, needs surfactant and ventilation
  • Failure to improve: think pneumothorax, pneumonia or sepsis, PPHN, cardiac disease
  • Hypoxemia on the ventilator: raise FiO2 and pressure support first
  • Tracheostomy: only for prolonged ventilator dependence or fixed airway obstruction
exam_pearl: Severe distress that does not settle is not the usual course of TTN: escalate support and look for another cause (pneumothorax, pneumonia, PPHN, cardiac disease).

stem: Newborn TTN, Hypoxia (he is receiving tx i don’t recall it but i think it was mechanical ventilator) Asking what indicates that he is deteriorating
OptC: O2 sat is not improving despite receiving o2
why_right: The question asks for a sign of deterioration in a newborn with TTN and hypoxia already on respiratory support. If "O2 sat is not improving despite receiving O2", oxygenation is failing even with treatment. That is direct evidence of worsening respiratory failure and means support must be escalated and the diagnosis reconsidered.
why_wrong_block:
A. A blood glucose of 55 mg/dL is within the acceptable range for a newborn and says nothing about the lungs. Glucose would only matter here if it were clearly low and the baby had symptoms.
B. TTN typically resolves over 24 to 72 hours, so symptoms still present at 24 hours are expected and not a sign of deterioration. It is persistence well beyond about 72 hours that should prompt you to look for another diagnosis.
key_concept:
In neonatal respiratory distress, deterioration means oxygenation or ventilation is failing on the current support.
  • Falling or static SpO2 despite O2: escalate support
  • Rising work of breathing, grunting, apnea: escalate support
  • TTN: usually better within 24 to 72 hours
  • Beyond about 72 hours, or worsening: think RDS, pneumonia, pneumothorax, PPHN
exam_pearl: A slow course of TTN is not deterioration; persistent hypoxemia despite O2 is.

stem: Newborn delivered Small for Gestational Age, what would you do next? (No additional information)
OptC: Close monitoring of glucose and thermal regulation
why_right: A small for gestational age newborn has limited glycogen and fat stores and a relatively large surface area. That puts the baby at risk of hypoglycemia and hypothermia in the first hours and days. With "no additional information" and no symptoms, the right step is anticipatory care: scheduled glucose checks, early feeding and close temperature control.
why_wrong_block:
A. Routine care without extra monitoring is right for an appropriately grown, well term baby. An SGA baby is at risk, and hypoglycemia can be silent, so it needs targeted screening.
B. Immediate IV glucose is for confirmed hypoglycemia that is symptomatic, severe or not responding to feeds. Giving it to an asymptomatic baby with no glucose result skips monitoring and early feeding.
key_concept:
At-risk newborns (SGA, LGA, infant of a diabetic mother, preterm) need anticipatory screening, not empirical treatment.
  • SGA risks: hypoglycemia, hypothermia, polycythemia
  • Steps: early feeding, warmth and skin to skin, scheduled glucose checks
  • Asymptomatic low glucose: feed, then recheck
  • Symptomatic or persistently low glucose: IV dextrose
exam_pearl: No symptoms and no glucose value yet: monitor and feed. A low reading with symptoms: IV glucose.

stem: Asthma child with recurrent symptoms of congested throat and mild fever with wheezing, the mother use inhaler as prescribed ،which important for the mother ?
OptA: Ensure the patient know how to use inhaler
why_right: This asthmatic child keeps having symptoms even though the inhaler is used "as prescribed". The most common fixable reason is poor inhaler technique, so you have to check that the child (and mother) can use the device properly. Watch them use it and correct it, usually with a spacer for a child, before stepping up medication or looking for another cause.
why_wrong_block: B. Vitamin C juice has no proven role in asthma control or in preventing viral triggers. It would distract from fixing the actual problem, which is drug delivery.
key_concept:
Before stepping up asthma treatment, check technique, adherence and triggers.
  • Uncontrolled asthma: check inhaler technique first (observe a demonstration)
  • Children: MDI with spacer (and mask if young)
  • Then check adherence, trigger exposure and comorbid rhinitis
  • Only then step up the controller
exam_pearl: "Uses the inhaler as prescribed" does not mean it is used correctly; technique is the first thing to check.

stem: A 2day old baby presents with lethargy, drowsiness, and vomiting. Glucose is normal. There is no acidosis and no ketones. Ammonia level is markedly elevated 420. What is the most appropriate next management?
why_right: A 2-day-old with lethargy, vomiting and drowsiness, normal glucose, no acidosis, no ketones and ammonia "markedly elevated 420" fits a urea cycle disorder. Ammonia at this level is neurotoxic, and each hour of exposure worsens brain injury. Dialysis (ideally hemodialysis) removes ammonia fastest, so it is the most appropriate management. Protein is stopped and IV glucose and nitrogen scavengers are started alongside it.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV glucose (with protein stopped) is part of the initial stabilization because it halts catabolism. However, it does not remove the ammonia already present, and glucose is normal here. On its own it is not enough at this ammonia level.
C. Sodium benzoate is a nitrogen scavenger that is given alongside dialysis or used alone for milder hyperammonemia. Its effect is too slow to be the sole treatment for a markedly high level in an encephalopathic neonate.
D. Lactulose lowers gut ammonia production and is used for hepatic encephalopathy in adults. It has no role in the acute treatment of neonatal urea cycle disorders.
key_concept:
In neonatal hyperammonemia, rule in a urea cycle disorder by the absence of acidosis and ketosis, then remove the ammonia fast.
  • High ammonia + no acidosis + normal glucose: urea cycle disorder
  • High ammonia + metabolic acidosis + ketosis: organic acidemia
  • Immediate steps: stop protein, give IV glucose (with or without insulin) to stop catabolism
  • Drugs: nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate), arginine
  • Markedly high or rising ammonia with encephalopathy: urgent hemodialysis
exam_pearl: Lactulose is for hepatic encephalopathy, not neonatal urea cycle crises; very high ammonia in an encephalopathic baby means dialysis.

stem: Kawasaki patient. And they said the dx And he used high aspirin and immunoglobulins And mentioned something about the carotid ( im not sure but it was CV system finding ) The what to give :
why_right: The child has already received the standard initial regimen of high-dose aspirin plus IVIG. A further cardiovascular finding (coronary involvement) or ongoing disease means the Kawasaki disease is refractory or high risk. In that situation, escalation with IV methylprednisolone is a recognised option to dampen vasculitis and protect the coronary arteries. That is why this recall keys IV steroid.
why_wrong_block: B. Low-dose oral aspirin is the routine antiplatelet step once the fever settles after IVIG, continued until echo follow-up is clear. It does not treat persistent inflammation, so it is not the answer when the stem signals refractory disease or coronary involvement.
key_concept:
Kawasaki disease: IVIG plus aspirin first, then escalate if the disease persists or the coronaries are involved.
  • Initial: IVIG plus moderate to high dose aspirin
  • After defervescence: low dose aspirin (antiplatelet)
  • Echocardiography: best test for the coronary arteries
  • IVIG resistant (persistent or recrudescent fever): second IVIG dose or IV methylprednisolone; infliximab is an alternative
  • Poor IVIG response predictors: high CRP, high neutrophils, low albumin, low sodium, high liver enzymes, age under 12 months
exam_pearl: If the stem describes only routine completion of therapy in an afebrile child, low dose aspirin fits; persistent disease or coronary involvement points to steroid escalation.

stem: Which of the following will increase epilepsy
why_right: A complex febrile seizure is focal, lasts longer than 15 minutes or recurs within 24 hours. It carries a clearly higher risk of later epilepsy than a simple febrile seizure. Other factors that add to the risk are a family history of epilepsy and abnormal neurodevelopment.
why_wrong_block: A. After a simple febrile seizure (generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, in a neurologically normal child), the risk of epilepsy is only slightly above that of the general population. Parents should be reassured that it does not cause epilepsy.
key_concept:
Febrile seizure: 6 months to 6 years, with fever, no CNS infection.
  • Simple: generalized, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours
  • Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours
  • Epilepsy risk: complex features, family history of epilepsy, developmental delay
  • Recurrence risk (a different question): younger age at first seizure, family history of febrile seizures, low fever at seizure
  • Management: treat the fever and its cause; reassure
exam_pearl: Do not confuse risk of recurrent febrile seizures with risk of epilepsy; complex features predict epilepsy.

stem: Pediatric with ankle and knee pain, limited range of motion, warmth, had gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago No Effusion (Mentioned On The Stem) How to MANAGE (It was management)
OptC: synovial aspiration for analysis and culture
why_right: Ankle and knee arthritis that began "2 weeks" after gastroenteritis is reactive arthritis, which is sterile and follows an enteric infection. The stem stresses "no effusion" and describes no fever or toxic picture, so septic arthritis is not suspected. The first-line management is an NSAID such as oral ibuprofen.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral prednisone is kept for reactive arthritis that does not respond to NSAIDs, or for severe disease (intra-articular steroid is another option). It is not first line.
C. Synovial aspiration is essential when a hot joint has an effusion and septic arthritis must be excluded, especially an acute single joint with fever. Here there is no effusion and the history points to a post-infectious arthritis.
D. IV antibiotics are the treatment for septic arthritis after the joint has been aspirated. Reactive arthritis is sterile, so antibiotics do not treat the joint inflammation.
key_concept:
Arthritis 1 to 4 weeks after a GI or GU infection is reactive arthritis: treat with an NSAID.
  • Reactive: oligoarthritis of the lower limbs after an enteric infection, sterile, NSAID first
  • Not responding: intra-articular or systemic steroid, then DMARD (sulfasalazine)
  • Septic: acute single hot joint, fever, effusion, refusal to move: aspirate, then IV antibiotics
  • JIA: arthritis over 6 weeks with morning stiffness
exam_pearl: Timing after gastroenteritis plus no effusion means reactive arthritis and an NSAID; fever with a hot joint effusion means aspirate first.

stem: Name of the reflex? (images: finger stroking infant's cheek/mouth, infant turning and opening mouth)
why_right: Stroking the infant's cheek or the corner of the mouth makes the baby turn the head toward the stimulus and open the mouth. That is the rooting reflex, which helps the baby find the nipple. It is present from birth.
why_wrong_block: B. The stepping reflex is elicited by holding the infant upright with the soles touching a surface, which produces alternating walking movements. It involves the legs, not the mouth.
key_concept:
Name the primitive reflex by its stimulus.
  • Cheek or corner of mouth stroked, head turns: rooting
  • Object placed in mouth: sucking
  • Feet on a surface while held upright: stepping
  • Head drop: Moro
  • Finger in the palm: palmar grasp
  • Head turned, fencing posture: ATNR
exam_pearl: Rooting is turning toward the touch; sucking needs something inside the mouth.

stem: Time of disappearance? (rooting reflex)
why_right: The rooting reflex is present at birth and normally disappears by about 4 months, when feeding comes under voluntary control.
why_wrong_block:
A. Disappearance at 2 months is too early for rooting. Around 2 to 3 months is when the asymmetrical tonic neck reflex fades.
C. Six months is when the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes disappear, not rooting.
key_concept:
Primitive reflex disappearance ages:
  • ATNR: about 2 to 3 months
  • Rooting and Galant: 4 months
  • Placing: 4 to 6 months
  • Moro and palmar grasp: 6 months
  • Babinski: 12 to 18 months
  • Parachute: appears at 8 to 10 months and persists for life
exam_pearl: Rooting goes at 4 months, Moro and grasp at 6; a reflex that persists beyond its window suggests a CNS problem.

stem: preterm. Now he has respiratory distress. Cause?
why_right: The decisive clue is the single word "preterm". Hyaline membrane disease (respiratory distress syndrome) is caused by surfactant deficiency in immature lungs, so a premature baby who develops respiratory distress (tachypnea, grunting, recessions, falling SpO2) shortly after birth has RDS until proven otherwise. The CXR would show diffuse ground glass (reticulogranular) opacities with air bronchograms.
why_wrong_block:
B. Meconium aspiration is a disease of term or post term babies born through meconium stained liquor, with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation on CXR; a preterm baby rarely passes meconium in utero.
C. Transient tachypnea of the newborn is due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, typically in a term baby delivered by C-section, mild and self resolving, with fluid in the fissures on CXR. Prematurity points to RDS instead.
D. Congenital heart disease presents with cyanosis out of proportion to respiratory effort, murmur, abnormal pulses or a failed hyperoxia test; nothing in the stem points to a cardiac lesion, and prematurity is the classic RDS clue.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress: the gestational age and delivery mode pick the diagnosis.
  • Preterm: RDS (surfactant deficiency), ground glass CXR
  • Term C-section: TTN (retained lung fluid), fluid in fissures, self limiting
  • Term or post term with meconium stained liquor: meconium aspiration, patchy infiltrates + hyperinflation
  • Maternal fever / prolonged rupture of membranes: pneumonia or sepsis
  • Cyanosis without much distress, murmur: congenital heart disease
exam_pearl: C-section favours TTN only in a term baby; once the stem says preterm (especially with significant hypoxia), RDS wins.

stem: A 32 y/o man presents to the ER after a motorcycle accident. He has multiple pelvic fractures, vascular injuries and they did surgery for him What is the most appropriate management post op
why_right: The lead-in is "management post op": the fractures and vascular injuries have already been fixed, so the priority shifts to recovery. Early mobilization and physiotherapy after pelvic fixation reduce DVT, pneumonia, pressure sores and joint stiffness and speed return of function in a young patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. A pelvic binder is a pre-hospital/ED measure to close an unstable pelvic ring and reduce bleeding before definitive fixation; after surgical fixation it has no role.
B. Analgesia and fluids are routine supportive care for every post-op patient, but they are not the specific management goal the question targets; fluids are the answer in the resuscitation phase.
C. Antibiotics are perioperative prophylaxis (or for open fractures/infection); there is no sign of infection here to justify ongoing broad-spectrum cover.
key_concept:
Pelvic trauma by phase: binder and resuscitation pre-op, fixation in theatre, mobilize early post-op.
  • ED: ABC, pelvic binder, blood products, angioembolization or packing if bleeding.
  • Theatre: fixation and vascular repair.
  • Post-op: early mobilization and physiotherapy, VTE prophylaxis, analgesia.
exam_pearl: Read the phase: "post op" removes the binder and resuscitation answers.

stem: Best type of dressing of planter of foot:
key_concept:
Choose the dressing by exudate and infection.
  • Dry/necrotic: hydrogel (adds moisture).
  • Low exudate, clean: hydrocolloid or film.
  • Moderate to heavy exudate: alginate or foam.
  • Infected: frequent-change dressings (gauze) plus treat infection.
  • Diabetic plantar ulcer: offloading matters more than dressing type.
exam_pearl: Wet wound gets an absorber (alginate/foam); dry wound gets a donor (hydrogel).

stem: DM with ulcer in the foot, what type of dressing?
why_right: Diabetic foot (plantar) ulcers are typically exudative (the embedded version says "plantar ulcer with exudate"), so the dressing should absorb fluid while keeping the bed moist. Alginate turns into a gel as it absorbs exudate, suits moderate to heavy drainage and is easy to change for frequent ulcer inspection.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hydrogel donates moisture to dry or necrotic wounds to soften slough; on an exudative ulcer it adds fluid and macerates the edges.
C. Hydrocolloid is occlusive and suits low exudate, clean wounds; on a diabetic ulcer it may conceal infection and is generally avoided.
D. Transparent film absorbs nothing; it is for dry superficial wounds or IV sites, not an exudative plantar ulcer.
key_concept:
Dressing by exudate: wet wound needs an absorber, dry wound needs moisture.
  • Heavy/moderate exudate: alginate, foam, hydrofiber.
  • Dry/necrotic: hydrogel.
  • Low exudate, clean: hydrocolloid, film.
  • Diabetic foot ulcer care: offloading, debridement, infection control and pulse/vascular check come first.
exam_pearl: If the stem says exudate, pick the absorber (alginate); hydrogel is the trap for dry wounds.

stem: A patient with spinal metastasis presents with rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence (level T something). His symptoms continue to worsen despite medical management. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: continue to worsen despite medical management
why_right: This is metastatic spinal cord compression with "rapidly progressive paraparesis" and sphincter loss ("fecal incontinence") that keeps worsening despite medical management (steroids). Progressive deficit despite steroids is the indication for urgent surgical decompression (usually with stabilization, followed by radiotherapy), which gives the best chance of preserving or regaining walking and continence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemotherapy acts too slowly to relieve an acute compression; it is used only for very chemosensitive tumors alongside definitive local treatment.
B. Steroids are the first step to reduce cord edema, but they have already failed here; escalating them does not decompress the cord.
C. Conservative care would be right only for a patient unfit for surgery or with very poor prognosis; with a progressing deficit it risks permanent paraplegia.
key_concept:
Metastatic cord compression: steroids immediately, MRI whole spine, then decompress.
  • Red flags: back pain, leg weakness, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction.
  • Immediate: high-dose dexamethasone.
  • Imaging: urgent MRI whole spine.
  • Progressive deficit, instability or failed medical therapy: urgent surgery then radiotherapy.
  • Unfit for surgery or radiosensitive tumor: radiotherapy.
exam_pearl: Worsening despite steroids is the trigger that turns the answer from radiotherapy/steroids to surgery.

stem: Child that has taken alkaline substance, presented 3 hours later, SOB and salivation
key_concept:
Caustic ingestion in a child: Airway, then perforation, then grading.
  • Stridor, hoarseness, respiratory distress: secure airway (intubation) first
  • Perforation signs (mediastinitis, peritonitis, free air, shock): surgery
  • Symptomatic but stable: admit, NPO, early endoscopy to grade injury
  • Asymptomatic, no oral lesions: observation, may be discharged
  • Never induce vomiting, never give neutralising agents, no blind NG tube
exam_pearl: Absence of oral burns does not exclude esophageal injury; symptoms (drooling, dysphagia, stridor) are what predict significant damage.

stem: A Child with inhalation of alkaline fluid 3h ago presented with oropharyngeal pain, difficulty swallowing, Drooling Of Saliva. Vitally stable, O/E oropharyngeal redness, mild tenderness. What to do?
OptC: Exploration of the area in OR
why_right: The child is "vitally stable" with only oropharyngeal redness and "mild tenderness", but has dysphagia and drooling 3 hours after alkali exposure (the stem says inhalation, but the picture is of ingestion). Drooling and dysphagia predict real mucosal injury, so the child cannot be sent home, yet there are no features of airway compromise or perforation that would need an emergency procedure. Admission for conservative care (NPO, IV fluids, airway monitoring, analgesia, with early endoscopy to grade injury) is the appropriate step.
why_wrong_block:
B. Emergency bronchoscopy is for suspected aspirated foreign body or airway injury with stridor or respiratory distress; this child has a stable airway and no respiratory signs.
C. Surgical exploration is reserved for perforation (mediastinitis, peritonitis, free air, shock); here vital signs are stable and findings are mild local redness and tenderness.
D. Discharge is only for a fully asymptomatic child with no oral lesions; drooling and difficulty swallowing are warning signs of esophageal injury and need inpatient monitoring.
key_concept:
Symptomatic but stable caustic ingestion = admit.
  • Airway signs (stridor, hoarseness, distress): secure airway first
  • Perforation signs: surgery
  • Drooling, dysphagia, vomiting with stable vitals: admit, NPO, supportive care, early endoscopy to grade
  • Asymptomatic, no oral burns: observe, may go home
  • Avoid induced vomiting, neutralisers and blind NG tubes
exam_pearl: Drooling and dysphagia mean injury even if the mouth looks only mildly red; never discharge a symptomatic caustic ingestion.

stem: A child was choking with a popcorn and then was removed by coughing After that he has hyperinflation of the right lower lobe and crackles or crepitations What to do next
highlight_terms_source: hyperinflation of the right lower lobe
why_right: A witnessed choking episode on "popcorn" followed by unilateral "hyperinflation of the right lower lobe" and crackles means a fragment is still lodged in the right bronchial tree, acting as a ball valve that lets air in but not out. Coughing relieved the acute choking but did not clear the airway. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the procedure of choice because it both confirms and removes the foreign body while keeping the airway controlled.
why_wrong_block:
B. Reassurance would be right only with a normal examination and normal imaging after the episode; here there are objective signs (unilateral hyperinflation, crackles) of a retained foreign body.
C. Observation delays removal and risks post obstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis or complete obstruction; a positive history plus focal signs is an indication for bronchoscopy, not watchful waiting.
D. Flexible bronchoscopy is useful diagnostically when suspicion is low or findings are equivocal, but it is poor for retrieving organic material in a child; with clear evidence of a retained foreign body, rigid bronchoscopy is preferred because it is therapeutic.
key_concept:
Suspected foreign body aspiration in a child.
  • History of choking is the most sensitive clue; cough may clear symptoms but not the object
  • Right main bronchus is the commonest site
  • CXR: ipsilateral hyperinflation (ball valve), mediastinal shift away; get expiratory films; CXR may be normal
  • Late: collapse, consolidation, recurrent pneumonia
  • Clear suspicion: rigid bronchoscopy (diagnostic and therapeutic)
  • Low suspicion or unclear: flexible bronchoscopy to look
exam_pearl: A choking episode that resolved with coughing does not exclude a retained foreign body; focal hyperinflation on one side means go to rigid bronchoscopy.

stem: 6 years old boy came to clinic with , Pale and Ecchymosis and petechiae post upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago boy now is well demarcated of bruising and petechiae. labs Low Platelets Low Hb Normal WBC Examiner: There Were Other Labs , But I Don't Remember Them what is most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis
highlight_terms_source: post upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago
why_right: Petechiae and bruising 2 weeks after a URTI suggest ITP, but ITP is a diagnosis of isolated thrombocytopenia. This child is "pale" with "low Hb" as well as low platelets, i.e. two cell lines affected, which raises concern for marrow failure or infiltration (leukemia, aplastic anemia). A bone marrow examination is the test that confirms the diagnosis in that situation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulation factor assays are for hemophilia or von Willebrand disease, which give deep bleeding or hemarthroses with a normal platelet count; this child's bleeding is petechial with low platelets.
C. EBV serology is relevant when there is fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes; it does not confirm the cause of anemia plus thrombocytopenia, and a malignancy must be excluded first.
key_concept:
Child with petechiae after a viral illness: count the cell lines.
  • Isolated low platelets, well child, normal Hb and WBC: ITP, clinical diagnosis, marrow not routinely needed
  • Two or more cytopenias, pallor, bone pain, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy: bone marrow examination (leukemia, aplastic anemia)
  • Normal platelets with deep or joint bleeding: coagulation factors (hemophilia)
  • ITP marrow, if done: increased megakaryocytes
exam_pearl: If Hb or WBC is also abnormal without an obvious bleeding cause, it is not simple ITP; examine the marrow to exclude leukemia or aplastic anemia.

stem: Child present with 7 week left knee morning stiffness, pain , warm , effusion, decrease rang of motion, , no systematic symptoms no fever or malais or other , blood and stool culture negative What is your diagnosis?
why_right: A single large joint (left knee) with "morning stiffness", warmth, effusion and reduced range of motion for "7 weeks", with no fever or systemic features and negative cultures, fits oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. JIA requires arthritis lasting 6 weeks or more in a child under 16 after excluding other causes, and the oligoarticular type involves 1 to 4 asymmetric large joints, typically the knee.
why_wrong_block:
B. Septic arthritis is acute (days), with fever, an ill child and severe pain or refusal to move the limb; 7 weeks of afebrile morning stiffness with negative blood culture does not fit.
C. Reactive arthritis is an asymmetric, mainly lower limb oligoarthritis that follows a GI or genitourinary infection, often with conjunctivitis or urethritis; the stem gives no preceding diarrhea or urethritis, and persistent arthritis beyond 6 weeks in a child points to JIA.
D. Hemophilia A causes acute hemarthrosis, often after minor trauma, in a boy with a bleeding history; it does not give weeks of inflammatory morning stiffness.
key_concept:
Chronic arthritis in a child = JIA (≥6 weeks, onset <16 years, other causes excluded).
  • Oligoarticular: 1 to 4 large joints (knee), young child, risk of asymptomatic uveitis, needs slit lamp screening
  • Polyarticular: 5 or more joints, symmetric
  • Systemic: quotidian fever, rash, organomegaly, serositis
  • Septic: acute, febrile, aspirate the joint
  • Reactive: 1 to 4 weeks after GI or GU infection, asymmetric lower limb, eye and urethral features
exam_pearl: Duration flips the answer: a hot knee for days with fever is septic; a swollen stiff knee for over 6 weeks without fever is oligoarticular JIA.

stem: During examination of a Newborn they found out right undescended testicle (in the inguinal canal) When should the surgery performed?
why_right: The baby is a "newborn" with a testis palpable in the inguinal canal. Many undescended testes descend spontaneously in the first few months of life, so the correct approach is to wait and re-examine; if the testis has not descended by about 6 months, spontaneous descent is unlikely and orchidopexy is done, ideally before 18 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate surgery in a newborn is unnecessary because spontaneous descent is common in early infancy; operating now exposes the baby to avoidable anaesthetic and surgical risk.
B. Waiting until after 2 years is too late; delayed orchidopexy worsens the risk of impaired fertility and makes malignancy harder to detect. Surgery should be done by about 18 months.
key_concept:
Undescended testis timeline.
  • Newborn: observe, re-examine over the first months
  • Not descended by about 6 months: refer, spontaneous descent unlikely
  • Palpable: orchidopexy, ideally 6 to 18 months
  • Non palpable: diagnostic laparoscopy
  • Hormonal therapy not recommended
  • Orchidopexy reduces infertility and torsion risk and allows self examination; it does not remove cancer risk
exam_pearl: Newborn = wait a few months; older infant or child with a persisting palpable testis = orchidopexy now, not "wait till puberty".

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. Physical examination reveals a palpable right upper quadrant mass. He has ascites that is well controlled with diuretic therapy. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrates a 6 × 6 cm mass in the right hepatic lobe with arterial phase enhancement. The portal venous and delayed phases are unremarkable. A biopsy of the lesion confirms hepatocellular carcinoma. What is the most appropriate management step at this stage?
key_concept:
HCC in cirrhosis: treatment follows tumour burden plus liver reserve.
  • Single mass <6 cm, good liver function: surgical resection
  • Single mass ≥6 cm or multiple masses, liver-confined: TACE
  • Within transplant criteria (Milan: single ≤5 cm, or up to 3 lesions ≤3 cm): liver transplant
  • Vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread: systemic therapy
  • Exam habit: if TACE is not among the options for a 6 cm lesion, choose resection
exam_pearl: Two near-identical recalls are keyed differently: the version stressing HBV cirrhosis with controlled ascites is keyed to TACE, while the version stressing a biopsy-proven 6 × 6 cm mass is keyed to resection; read for liver reserve.

stem: A 42-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis evaluated for focal lesion at US abdomen. He is asymptomatic. Currently on diuretics with well-controlled ascites (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values: Hb 110 (130-170 g/L Male; 120-160 g/L Female); Platelets count 123 (150-400 x 109/L); INR 1.5 (0.8-1.2); Total bilirubin 16 (3.5-16.5 mol/L); Aspartate aminotransferase 98 (12-40 IU/L); Alanine aminotransferase 65 (5-40 IU/L); Alkaline phosphatase 120 (39-117 IU/L); Albumin 30 (34-56 g/L). CT scan of liver: Demonstrated a 6 cm lesion with arterial enhancement at RT lobe, portal vein and hepatic veins were patent. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
why_right: A focal arterially enhancing lesion in a hepatitis B cirrhotic liver is HCC. It is a single "6 cm lesion" with "portal vein and hepatic veins patent" (no vascular invasion), so it is intermediate, liver-confined disease. A single mass of 6 cm or more is treated with transarterial chemoembolisation, especially since the liver reserve is reduced (albumin 30, INR 1.5, ascites on diuretics, platelets 123), making resection unsafe.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sorafenib is systemic therapy for advanced HCC with vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread; here the veins are patent and the tumour is confined to the liver.
B. Transplant is for HCC within Milan criteria (single lesion ≤5 cm, or up to 3 lesions each ≤3 cm); a single 6 cm lesion is outside them.
C. Resection suits a single mass under 6 cm with well-preserved liver function; this lesion is 6 cm and the patient has ascites, low albumin, raised INR and thrombocytopenia, signs of portal hypertension and limited reserve.
key_concept:
HCC treatment by size and spread:
  • Single mass <6 cm, good liver function: resection
  • Within Milan criteria with cirrhosis: transplant
  • Single mass ≥6 cm or multiple, liver-confined: TACE
  • Vascular invasion or metastasis: sorafenib / systemic therapy
  • Arterial enhancement with washout in a cirrhotic liver is diagnostic without biopsy
exam_pearl: Patent portal and hepatic veins rule out the advanced stage, so a 6 cm single lesion goes to TACE, not sorafenib.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot; answer marked with ** before D.

stem: A previously healthy child presents with a febrile seizure associated with an upper respiratory tract infection. The mother is concerned about recurrence and asks about prevention strategies. What is the most appropriate advice?
OptA: Give regular doses of ibuprofen during febrile illnesses
OptC: Perform an EEG to identify type of seizure
OptD: Educate the family about seizure first aid and management
why_right: A "previously healthy" child with a seizure during a febrile URTI has a simple febrile seizure, which is benign, does not cause brain damage and usually does not lead to epilepsy. No intervention has been shown to prevent recurrence with an acceptable risk benefit balance, so the most appropriate advice to a mother asking about "prevention" is reassurance plus education: positioning, timing the seizure, not putting anything in the mouth, and when to call for help or use a rescue medication if prescribed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Regular antipyretics (ibuprofen or paracetamol) during febrile illnesses make the child more comfortable but do not reduce the recurrence of febrile seizures.
B. Continuous antiepileptic drugs can reduce recurrences but their adverse effects outweigh the benefit in simple febrile seizures, and they do not prevent later epilepsy; they are not recommended.
C. EEG is not indicated after a simple febrile seizure in a neurologically normal child; it does not predict recurrence or later epilepsy. It is considered for atypical or complex features.
key_concept:
Simple febrile seizure: reassure and educate.
  • Age about 6 months to 6 years, fever, generalized, brief, once in 24 hours, normal child
  • No routine EEG, imaging or bloods beyond finding the fever source
  • No prophylactic antiepileptics
  • Antipyretics for comfort only, they do not prevent recurrence
  • Teach seizure first aid; rescue benzodiazepine for prolonged seizures if advised
  • Complex (focal, prolonged, recurrent in 24 hours): further evaluation
exam_pearl: Antipyretics treat the fever, not the seizure risk; when the mother asks about prevention, the answer is education.

stem: A patient presents with a mass in the triceps region that has been progressively increasing in size over the past 3 months. MRI findings raise a strong suspicion for malignancy. What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: progressively increasing in size over the past 3 months
why_right: A "progressively increasing" mass in the triceps (a limb soft tissue mass) with MRI "strong suspicion for malignancy" is a suspected soft tissue sarcoma. The biopsy of choice is an image-guided core needle biopsy placed along the line of the future resection: it gives intact tissue for subtype and grade while limiting tumour seeding, and the tract is excised with the definitive operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fine needle aspiration gives only cells without tissue architecture, so it cannot reliably type and grade a sarcoma; it suits cystic or thyroid lesions and lymph nodes.
B. Excising a suspected sarcoma before diagnosis (the unplanned "whoops" excision) leaves inadequate margins and compromises the definitive resection; excisional biopsy suits only small, superficial lesions.
C. Open incisional biopsy contaminates tissue planes and risks haematoma and spillage; it is reserved for when core biopsy is nondiagnostic.
key_concept:
Suspected limb sarcoma pathway:
  • Imaging: MRI of the mass
  • Diagnosis: image-guided core needle biopsy along the planned resection line
  • Staging: CT chest (lungs are the main metastatic site)
  • Incisional biopsy only if core is nondiagnostic
  • Never shell out the mass first
exam_pearl: Large, deep or growing limb mass = sarcoma until proven otherwise; core biopsy, not excision.

stem: A 42-year-old man is involved in a high-speed motor vehicle accident. He presents with shortness of breath, respiratory rate 32/min, and paradoxical chest wall movement. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: "Paradoxical chest wall movement" after high-speed blunt trauma is flail chest (two or more adjacent ribs each fractured in two or more places). The real threat is pain-limited breathing and the underlying pulmonary contusion, so management is supportive: good analgesia and respiratory support (oxygen, escalating to ventilation if he tires or becomes hypoxic, as the RR of 32 suggests may happen).
why_wrong_block:
A. Needle thoracostomy treats tension pneumothorax (hypotension, raised JVP, tracheal shift, hyperresonance); none of those signs are described.
B. A chest tube drains a pneumothorax or haemothorax; flail chest alone does not need one unless an associated air or blood collection is found.
D. A three-sided occlusive dressing is for an open (sucking) chest wound; this is blunt trauma with an intact chest wall.
key_concept:
Chest trauma: match the sign to the fix.
  • Paradoxical movement = flail chest: analgesia, oxygen, ventilation if failing
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
  • Simple pneumothorax or haemothorax: chest tube
  • Open (sucking) wound: three-sided dressing then chest tube
  • Chest tube output >1500 ml initially: thoracotomy
exam_pearl: Flail chest kills through the contusion underneath and hypoventilation from pain, so analgesia is treatment, not comfort.

stem: 65 years old woman came to the ER complaining of sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back Xray: widened mediastinum Dx?
highlight_terms_source: sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back
why_right: "Sudden" severe pain radiating to the back in an older woman plus a "widened mediastinum" on chest X-ray is aortic dissection until proven otherwise. A descending thoracic dissection can present as epigastric or interscapular pain, and mediastinal widening reflects the dilated, dissected aorta. Confirm with CT angiography if stable, or echocardiography if unstable.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oesophageal rupture can widen the mediastinum, but it follows forceful vomiting or endoscopy and shows pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema or pleural effusion; no such history is given.
C. GERD gives burning retrosternal discomfort related to meals and lying down, never sudden severe pain or a widened mediastinum.
D. Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back too, but after gallstones or alcohol, with vomiting and raised lipase; it does not widen the mediastinum.
key_concept:
Back-radiating epigastric/chest pain: the X-ray decides.
  • Widened mediastinum, sudden tearing pain: aortic dissection
  • Pneumomediastinum after vomiting: Boerhaave rupture
  • Normal chest X-ray, gallstones/alcohol, high lipase: pancreatitis
  • Pulsatile abdominal mass: AAA
  • Dissection imaging: CT angiography (stable), echo (unstable)
exam_pearl: Epigastric pain to the back usually says pancreatitis, but a widened mediastinum moves the answer to the aorta.

stem: A newborn presents with abdominal distention, tenderness, absent bowel sounds, and no meconium passage for 48 hours. On examination, a sudden gush of stool occurs after a digital rectal exam, and the baby becomes stable. What is the most appropriate initial next step?
highlight_terms_source: sudden gush of stool occurs after a digital rectal exam
why_right: "No meconium passage for 48 hours" with abdominal distension and a "sudden gush of stool" after the digital rectal exam (squirt sign) is the classic picture of Hirschsprung disease. The diagnosis is confirmed by rectal biopsy (suction biopsy in a neonate) showing absent ganglion cells, and it is the option that leads to definitive diagnosis and surgical planning.
why_wrong_block: B. A glycerin suppository suits meconium plug syndrome or simple functional constipation; using it here only gives temporary decompression and delays the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease, which carries a risk of enterocolitis.
key_concept:
Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic distal bowel).
  • Delayed meconium beyond 24 to 48 hours, distension, bilious vomiting
  • DRE: tight sphincter, empty rectum, explosive gush of stool (squirt sign)
  • Initial imaging: abdominal X-ray, contrast enema (transition zone)
  • Confirmatory, gold standard: rectal (suction) biopsy, absent ganglion cells
  • Treatment: resection of the aganglionic segment (pull through)
  • Danger: Hirschsprung enterocolitis
exam_pearl: If contrast enema or X-ray is offered as the "initial" test it is chosen first; when only biopsy is offered against a symptomatic remedy, choose rectal biopsy.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0899).
Compiler note: Q restatement (newborn, distention, no meconium 48hrs, gush of stool after DRE, stable; most appropriate next step?) highlights A. Suction and rectal biopsy (vs B. US).

stem: 72 years old male known to have hypertension and is heavy smoker was found incidentally to have abdominal pulsatile mass. Ultrasound abdomen: 4.5cm abdominal aortic aneurysm Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: An "incidentally" found, asymptomatic 4.5 cm AAA in a man is below the elective repair threshold (5.5 cm in men). The correct plan is surveillance with serial ultrasound to track growth, together with risk factor control (stop smoking, control BP). Repair is triggered by reaching threshold size, rapid growth, symptoms or rupture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simple reassurance ignores a real aneurysm that can grow and rupture; it needs scheduled imaging and risk factor control, not discharge.
B. Urgent surgery is for a symptomatic (tender, painful) or ruptured AAA; elective repair is for ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5 cm in women) or rapid growth. This one is asymptomatic and 4.5 cm.
D. Endarterectomy removes atherosclerotic plaque from a stenosed artery (e.g. carotid); it is not an aneurysm operation. AAA repair is open graft replacement or EVAR.
key_concept:
AAA management by size and symptoms:
  • Asymptomatic, below threshold: ultrasound surveillance + stop smoking + BP control
  • Repair: ≥5.5 cm men, ≥5 cm women, rapid growth, or symptomatic
  • Ruptured / unstable: straight to theatre (bedside US if needed)
  • Initial imaging: ultrasound; stable symptomatic: CT angiography
exam_pearl: Tenderness or pain turns the same 4.5 cm aneurysm into an urgent repair.

stem: A patient with chronic limb ischemia (history of intermittent claudication relieved by rest) presents with acute leg pain and diminished pulses. What is the best initial test?
why_right: Known claudication plus new "acute leg pain and diminished pulses" is acute on chronic limb ischaemia. After starting heparin, the "best initial test" is Doppler ultrasound: it is bedside, fast and non-invasive, confirming loss of arterial flow and locating the occlusion. CT angiography then maps the arteries for revascularisation.
why_wrong_block:
A. ABI is the first test for stable chronic PAD (claudication); in an acute presentation it does not localise the occlusion or guide urgent treatment.
C. MR angiography is slower, less available, and reserved for when iodinated contrast is contraindicated; not an initial test.
D. CT angiography is the confirmatory, gold standard test (the answer to "most appropriate" or "confirmatory" investigation), not the initial one.
key_concept:
Limb ischaemia imaging ladder:
  • Chronic PAD: ABI first, then duplex US, then CT angiography
  • Acute ischaemia: heparin, then Doppler US (initial), then CT angiography (gold standard)
  • Paralysed/threatened limb: skip imaging, go to revascularisation
  • 6 Ps: pain, pallor, paraesthesia, pulselessness, perishing cold, paralysis
exam_pearl: "Initial" = Doppler, "most appropriate/confirmatory" = CT angiography; a paralysed limb gets no imaging at all.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q restatement: K/C DM HTN and PAD, sudden onset leg pain and paresthesia, diminished pulse; most appropriate initial investigation? A. CT Angiography B. ABI C. Doppler. Answer: C (Doppler).

stem: Man presents with progressive shortness of breath for the past 5 days. He was involved in a traffic accident 2 weeks ago. On examination, breath sounds are absent on the right side. with pic of chest X-ray showing a homogenous white appearance on the base of right lung looks like hemothorax. His respiratory rate is 24/min and oxygen saturation is 90% rest of vitals are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: breath sounds are absent on the right side
homogenous white appearance on the base of right lung
why_right: Progressive dyspnoea "2 weeks" after a road traffic accident with "absent breath sounds" on the right and a white (opacified) right base is a delayed traumatic haemothorax, causing hypoxia (SpO2 90%, RR 24). A post-traumatic pleural collection large enough to cause symptoms is drained with a chest tube (tube thoracostomy) after ABCDE, which also lets you measure the blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. There is no fever or infective picture; antibiotics alone would treat empyema or pneumonia but not drain blood compressing the lung.
B. Needle aspiration is used for a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax (and needle decompression for tension pneumothorax with hypotension and tracheal shift); a needle cannot effectively drain a traumatic haemothorax.
D. Thoracic surgery (thoracotomy or VATS) is for massive haemothorax (>1500 ml on tube insertion, or about 200 ml/hour for 2 to 4 hours), instability, or a retained clotted collection after a chest tube, not as the first step.
key_concept:
Traumatic pleural collections:
  • Haemothorax or simple traumatic pneumothorax: ABCDE then chest tube
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
  • Thoracotomy: >1500 ml on insertion, about 200 ml/hour for 2 to 4 hours, or decompensation
  • Retained clotted haemothorax after tube: VATS
exam_pearl: White hemithorax base after trauma = blood; dark hemithorax with no lung markings = air. Both start with a chest tube unless tension.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall mentions a chest X-ray picture, not reproduced on the page.
