stem: A 3-year-old child presents with high-grade fever and sore throat. On examination, there is a diffuse erythematous “sandpaper-like” rash. A rapid antigen detection test is positive. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: rapid antigen detection test is positive
why_right: High fever, sore throat and a diffuse "sandpaper-like" rash is scarlet fever, a group A streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis with an erythrogenic toxin rash. The positive rapid antigen detection test confirms GAS, so antibiotics are indicated. Oral amoxicillin (or penicillin V) for a full 10 days is first line; the full course eradicates the organism from the pharynx and prevents acute rheumatic fever.
why_wrong_block:
A. Supportive treatment only: right for viral pharyngitis with a NEGATIVE rapid test and mild findings; a confirmed GAS infection must be treated to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
B. Acyclovir for 7 days: treats herpes simplex (e.g. herpetic gingivostomatitis with gum involvement) or varicella; it has no activity against streptococci.
key_concept:
Scarlet fever = GAS pharyngitis + toxin rash; confirm then treat with a 10 day course.
  • Clues: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, flushed face with circumoral pallor, Pastia lines, later desquamation
  • Diagnosis: rapid antigen test first, throat culture to confirm a negative result
  • Treatment: oral amoxicillin or penicillin V for 10 days
  • Penicillin allergy: macrolide or first generation cephalosporin (if not anaphylactic)
  • Goal of full course: prevent acute rheumatic fever
exam_pearl: Positive rapid test = treat; negative rapid test with mild viral features = supportive care (send culture in children if suspicion remains).

stem: A term newborn with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is admitted to the NICU for close monitoring due to risk of complications. Which of the following complications is most likely?
why_right: An IUGR newborn has poor glycogen, fat and mineral reserves and is often exposed to chronic placental insufficiency and perinatal hypoxia. Among the listed options, hypocalcemia is the recognised metabolic complication (early neonatal hypocalcemia is linked to perinatal asphyxia and growth restriction). The classic IUGR list is hypoglycemia, hypothermia, hypocalcemia and polycythemia, so only C fits here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hyperthermia: IUGR babies get HYPOthermia because of reduced subcutaneous fat and a large surface area relative to weight.
B. Hyperglycemia: IUGR babies get HYPOglycemia from low glycogen stores; neonatal hyperglycemia is more a problem of extremely preterm infants on IV dextrose.
D. Anemia: chronic fetal hypoxia raises erythropoietin, so IUGR babies get POLYCYTHEMIA (with hyperviscosity and jaundice), not anemia.
key_concept:
IUGR newborn complications: think "low reserves + chronic hypoxia".
  • Hypoglycemia (low glycogen)
  • Hypothermia (low fat)
  • Hypocalcemia (perinatal asphyxia)
  • Polycythemia / hyperviscosity (chronic hypoxia raises EPO)
  • Perinatal asphyxia and meconium aspiration
exam_pearl: Every option is a mirror image of a true IUGR complication; flip hyper to hypo and anemia to polycythemia.

stem: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents to the emergency department with hypotension and tachycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: After trauma, "hypotension and tachycardia" is haemorrhagic (hypovolaemic) shock until proven otherwise; it is by far the commonest shock in trauma. Blood loss triggers a reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction (pale, cold peripheries), so start haemorrhage control and blood product resuscitation and look for the bleeding source.
why_wrong_block: A. Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury: loss of sympathetic tone gives hypotension with a normal or slow heart rate and warm, dry peripheries, often with a neurological deficit. Tachycardia argues against it.
key_concept:
Trauma shock by heart rate and skin:
  • Hypotension + tachycardia + cold, pale skin: haemorrhagic shock
  • Hypotension + bradycardia/normal HR + warm skin: neurogenic shock
  • Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds: tamponade
  • Hypotension + raised JVP + tracheal shift: tension pneumothorax
exam_pearl: The heart rate is the switch: fast = bleeding, slow with warm skin = cord injury.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot variant: '72. Pt had RTA he is hypotensive pale and has cold extremities, his HR is 120, what is the diagnosis? A) Neurogenic shock B) Hemorrhagic shock. Answer: B short case like this.'

stem: 67-year-old male presents with hematuria. Known BPH (prostate enlarged on exam, no suspicious features). No trauma, stones, flank pain, or systemic symptoms. IV pyelogram normal. Question: Next diagnostic test?
why_right: Haematuria in a 67-year-old man needs both the upper tract and the bladder examined to exclude malignancy, even with known BPH. The upper tract has already been cleared ("IV pyelogram normal"), and with no stones, flank pain or suspicious prostate, the remaining source to exclude is bladder (urothelial) cancer, which only cystoscopy visualises reliably. BPH is accepted as the cause of haematuria only after this workup.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT (CT urography) images the kidneys and ureters; the upper tract is already covered by the normal pyelogram, and CT misses small flat bladder lesions.
C. Ultrasound assesses kidneys, residual volume and prostate size but is insensitive for small bladder tumours; it does not replace cystoscopy.
D. Prostate biopsy is for a suspicious DRE or raised PSA; the prostate here is benign-feeling with "no suspicious features".
key_concept:
Adult haematuria workup = upper tract imaging + lower tract cystoscopy.
  • Upper tract: CT urography (older exams: IVP) or ultrasound
  • Lower tract: cystoscopy (bladder cancer)
  • Biggest risks: older age, male, smoking
  • Prostate biopsy only for abnormal DRE or raised PSA
  • BPH as the cause is a diagnosis of exclusion
exam_pearl: A normal upper tract study never ends a haematuria workup in an older man; the bladder still needs a scope.

stem: 50 old male age came to the clinic concerned seeing blood in his urine. While obtaining history the patient complained of Right Flank pain. No history of trauma or History Of Prior stones. On examination there's right flank tenderness and enlarged prostate On DRE. Urinalysis : 20 RBC What is The most appropriate investigation
why_right: Hematuria with "right flank pain" and "right flank tenderness" points to an upper tract cause, most commonly a ureteric or renal stone, even with no prior stones. Non-contrast CT KUB is the first line and most accurate imaging for suspected urolithiasis: it detects almost all stones regardless of composition and shows size, site, hydronephrosis and alternative causes. The enlarged prostate is a distractor; it does not explain flank pain.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cystoscopy looks at the bladder and urethra; it is the test for painless hematuria in an older patient (bladder cancer workup), not the first test when flank pain points to the kidney or ureter.
C. Plain X-ray KUB misses radiolucent (uric acid), small or overlying stones; it is used to follow known radiopaque stones, not to make the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Flank pain + hematuria = stone until proven otherwise: image with non-contrast CT KUB.
  • Suspected stone: non-contrast CT KUB (contrast can hide stones)
  • Pregnancy or children: ultrasound first
  • X-ray KUB: follow-up of known radiopaque stones
  • Painless hematuria in older adult: cystoscopy plus upper tract imaging
  • BPH symptoms alone: alpha blocker, cystoscopy only if bladder pathology suspected
exam_pearl: Painful (flank) hematuria = CT KUB; painless hematuria in an older man = think bladder cancer and cystoscopy.

stem: Pediatric girl complain of lef knee pain and joint swelling and chest pain on exercise, patient had sore throat three weeks ago treated with corticosteroids. Mother is asking how to prevent, Which of the following will prevent recurrence of this ?
why_right: Joint pain and swelling plus exertional chest pain three weeks after a sore throat that was not treated with antibiotics ("treated with corticosteroids") is acute rheumatic fever with possible carditis. The mother asks how to prevent recurrence, which is secondary prophylaxis: intramuscular benzathine penicillin given monthly. Duration depends on carditis: at least 5 years or to age 21 without carditis, longer if the heart was involved.
why_wrong_block:
A. 10 days of oral penicillin: this eradicates GAS from the throat in an acute pharyngitis (primary prevention, and also given once at ARF diagnosis); it does not protect against future infections and recurrences.
C. Strep vaccine: no group A streptococcal vaccine is available for clinical use, so it cannot be offered.
D. Flu vaccine: protects against influenza, not group A streptococcus; it has no role in preventing rheumatic fever recurrence.
key_concept:
Rheumatic fever: primary prevention treats the sore throat, secondary prevention stops recurrence.
  • Primary: 10 days oral penicillin or amoxicillin for GAS pharyngitis
  • Secondary: monthly IM benzathine penicillin
  • No carditis: 5 years or until age 21 (whichever longer)
  • Carditis, no residual disease: 10 years or until age 21
  • Carditis with residual valve disease: 10 years or until age 40, sometimes lifelong
  • Symptomatic treatment of arthritis: high dose aspirin
exam_pearl: "Prevent recurrence" = monthly benzathine penicillin; "prevent the first attack" = treat the strep throat for 10 days.

stem: An patient had a sigmoid polyp and was removed completely by endoscopy, which of the following will indicates the highest malignant transformation?
why_right: The question asks which histology carries the "highest malignant transformation". Among colorectal polyps, villous adenoma has the greatest malignant potential, ranking above tubulovillous and tubular adenomas, while hyperplastic polyps are non-neoplastic.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tubular adenoma is the most common adenoma but has the lowest malignant risk of the three adenoma types (ranks third).
C. Hyperplastic polyps are non-neoplastic and carry the lowest risk of all the options.
D. Tubulovillous adenoma has intermediate risk (ranks second), below a pure villous adenoma.
key_concept:
Malignant potential rises with the villous component.
  • 1) Villous adenoma: highest
  • 2) Tubulovillous adenoma
  • 3) Tubular adenoma
  • 4) Hyperplastic polyp: non-neoplastic, lowest
  • Size and high-grade dysplasia also raise risk
exam_pearl: Tubular = most common adenoma; villous = most malignant. Do not swap them.

stem: Newborn with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy What's the Maternal cause ?
why_right: Maternal diabetes mellitus causes fetal hyperglycemia and compensatory fetal hyperinsulinemia; insulin acts as a growth factor on the myocardium, producing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, typically asymmetric septal hypertrophy that can cause outflow obstruction. It usually regresses over the first months of life as insulin levels normalise.
why_wrong_block: A. SLE: maternal anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies cross the placenta and damage the conduction system, causing congenital complete heart block (neonatal lupus), not myocardial hypertrophy.
key_concept:
Maternal condition to neonatal heart lesion:
  • Diabetes: hypertrophic (septal) cardiomyopathy, transposition of great arteries, VSD, caudal regression
  • SLE (anti-Ro/La): congenital complete heart block
  • Lithium: Ebstein anomaly
  • Rubella: PDA, peripheral pulmonary stenosis
exam_pearl: Newborn heart BLOCK = mother with lupus; newborn THICK septum = mother with diabetes.

stem: An adult, medically free patient presents with upper abdominal pain for 12 hours associated with nausea, but no vomiting. There are no changes in stool or urine color, no pale stools or dark urine, and no changes in bowel habits. On examination, sclera and skin are normal. On deep palpation there is tenderness. Vital signs: normal Ultrasound findings: • Multiple gallbladder stones • Normal gallbladder wall thickness • No pericholecystic fluid • Common bile duct (CBD) is obstructed by a stone Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Common bile duct (CBD) is obstructed by a stone
why_right: A gallstone obstructing the "common bile duct" with 12 hours of upper abdominal pain, nausea and deep tenderness is the classic setup for gallstone (biliary) pancreatitis, the most common cause of acute pancreatitis. The other options are excluded by the stem: normal gallbladder wall and no pericholecystic fluid argue against cholecystitis, and normal sclera and skin with no dark urine or pale stool argue against obstructive jaundice. The diagnosis is confirmed with lipase or amylase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Acute cholecystitis needs ultrasound signs of inflammation (thick gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid) plus fever and RUQ tenderness; here the wall is normal, there is no fluid and vitals are normal.
C. Obstructive jaundice would show yellow sclera, dark urine, pale stools and itching; the stem explicitly says sclera and skin are normal with no urine or stool change.
D. Small bowel obstruction presents with colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation; this patient has no vomiting and no change in bowel habit, and ultrasound shows a biliary cause.
key_concept:
Gallstones on US: read the findings to name the complication.
  • Stones only, short pain, no signs: biliary colic
  • Thick wall + pericholecystic fluid + fever: acute cholecystitis
  • CBD stone + jaundice, dark urine, pale stool: choledocholithiasis / obstructive jaundice
  • Jaundice + fever + RUQ pain: ascending cholangitis
  • CBD stone + epigastric pain, no jaundice: gallstone pancreatitis (confirm with lipase)
exam_pearl: Pancreatitis needs 2 of 3: typical pain, lipase/amylase ≥3 times normal, imaging; a CBD stone with epigastric pain points there.

stem: Neoborn with delayed umbilical cord separation , the same thing happened with his older brother, normal PT , normal PTT and normal bleeding time but clot lysis take 5 hours?
highlight_terms_source: normal PT , normal PTT and normal bleeding time
why_right: The stem gives a newborn with an umbilical cord problem, an affected older brother, normal PT, PTT and bleeding time and an abnormal clot lysis test. Factor XIII cross-links and stabilises fibrin; without it the clot forms normally (so all screening tests are normal) but is unstable and dissolves abnormally fast in the clot solubility (urea) test. Its classic neonatal sign is prolonged bleeding from the umbilical stump, and it is autosomal recessive, fitting an affected sibling. Strictly, delayed cord separation is the textbook clue for leukocyte adhesion deficiency, but that is not an option and only factor XIII fits the normal screen plus abnormal clot lysis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Von Willebrand disease: mucosal bleeding (gums, epistaxis, menorrhagia) with a prolonged bleeding time and often a prolonged PTT from low factor VIII; here both are normal.
C. Bernard-Soulier syndrome: platelet adhesion defect (GPIb) with giant platelets, low count and a prolonged bleeding time; bleeding time is normal here.
D. Hemophilia: X-linked factor VIII or IX deficiency with a prolonged PTT and joint bleeding; a normal PTT excludes it even though a brother is affected.
key_concept:
All screening tests normal + bleeding = factor XIII deficiency (or a fibrinolysis disorder).
  • Prolonged BT only: platelet problem (vWD, Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann)
  • Prolonged PTT only: VIII, IX, XI, XII (hemophilia, vWD)
  • Prolonged PT only: factor VII
  • Both PT and PTT: common pathway or vitamin K deficiency
  • All normal: factor XIII, check clot solubility test
exam_pearl: Delayed cord SEPARATION with omphalitis and high neutrophils is leukocyte adhesion deficiency; umbilical stump BLEEDING with normal coagulation tests is factor XIII deficiency.

stem: 50 years old have pancreatitis 6 weeks ago came with worsening abdominal pain and palpable enlarging mass. CT scan : well defined fluid cyst. Most appropriate management ?
why_right: A "well defined fluid cyst" appearing "6 weeks" after pancreatitis is a pancreatic pseudocyst. It is symptomatic ("worsening abdominal pain") and growing ("palpable enlarging mass"), and it is at least 6 weeks old, so it meets the criteria for drainage. With no fever or leukocytosis to suggest infection, endoscopic internal drainage into the stomach or duodenum is the treatment of choice.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV antibiotics treat infection; there is no fever, leukocytosis or gas in the collection, and antibiotics do not decompress a pseudocyst.
C. Antibiotics plus observation is wrong twice: no infection is present, and observation is only for small, asymptomatic or early collections, not an enlarging symptomatic one.
D. Surgical drainage (cystgastrostomy) is reserved for failure or unsuitability of endoscopic drainage; it is not first line and not "immediate".
key_concept:
Post-pancreatitis collection: decide by size, age, symptoms and infection.
  • Pseudocyst: homogeneous, thin-walled, more than 4 weeks after pancreatitis; CT is the best imaging
  • Small, asymptomatic or under 6 weeks: observe
  • Over 6 cm, over 6 weeks, symptomatic or growing: endoscopic drainage
  • Infected pseudocyst or abscess (fever, high WBC, gas): percutaneous drainage first
  • Surgery: after failed minimally invasive drainage
exam_pearl: Same cyst plus fever and high WBC = abscess or infected collection, and the answer flips to percutaneous drainage.

stem: 4 years old has family history of essential hypertension and the parents are concerned on how to prevent or protect the kid?
why_right: A healthy 4 year old with only a family history of essential hypertension needs surveillance, not treatment. Blood pressure should be checked routinely (at least yearly from age 3) with age, sex and height percentiles, so that rising BP is detected early; this is combined with healthy lifestyle advice (activity, healthy weight, limited salt).
why_wrong_block:
A. Discouraging physical activity: the opposite of advice; regular exercise and a healthy weight lower the risk of hypertension.
B. Normal salt intake: does not protect; lifestyle advice for an at-risk child is to limit added salt, and diet alone does not replace BP monitoring.
C. Start antihypertensive: never indicated for a normotensive child; drugs are used only for confirmed hypertension (e.g. stage 2, symptomatic, or not controlled by lifestyle).
key_concept:
Child at risk of essential hypertension = monitor BP + lifestyle.
  • Routine BP measurement yearly from age 3
  • Interpret with age, sex and height percentiles
  • Lifestyle: activity, healthy weight, reduced salt
  • Drugs only for confirmed hypertension
  • Young child with high BP: look for secondary causes (renal, coarctation)
exam_pearl: Family history alone never justifies medication; the answer is surveillance.

stem: A young girl with RLQ abdominal pain, afebrile, normal WBC, mild tenderness, question specifically says: what is the most important management to avoid missed diagnosis?
OptA: Admit for serial abdominal examination and reassessment for 24 hours
OptB: Discharge and ask her to come back if pain returned
why_right: An "afebrile" girl with RLQ pain, "normal WBC" and only "mild tenderness" is an equivocal case of possible early appendicitis. The lead-in asks how to "avoid missed diagnosis": the safest strategy is admission for active observation with repeated abdominal examination by the same team, which reveals evolving appendicitis while avoiding an unnecessary operation. In a girl, a pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound are usually added during this period.
why_wrong_block:
B. Discharging an equivocal RLQ pain risks missing early appendicitis that progresses to perforation; discharge with return advice fits only clearly non-surgical, resolving pain.
C. Analgesia should be given and does not mask appendicitis, but on its own it does not establish or exclude the diagnosis; it is part of care, not the strategy that prevents a miss.
key_concept:
Equivocal RLQ pain: observe, re-examine, then decide.
  • Clear clinical appendicitis: surgery
  • Equivocal (mild signs, normal WBC, afebrile): admit, serial exams and labs
  • Female: pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound (torsion, ovarian cyst, ectopic)
  • Children and pregnancy: ultrasound first; CT if still unclear in adults
  • Analgesia is safe and does not hide peritonitis
exam_pearl: Serial examination is the best tool for an unclear appendix; analgesia is safe and should never be withheld while observing.

stem: 2 month old child was found to have an ejection systolic murmur on clinical examination. The mother reports SOB on exertion with physical activity. There is no history of chest pain nor syncope. ECHO confirmed aortic stenosis with good left ventricular systolic function. Aortic valve gradient of 60 mmH. BP and HR are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
why_right: This infant has aortic stenosis that is symptomatic ("SOB on exertion") with a significant gradient (60 mmHg), so intervention is indicated rather than observation. In infants and children the first-line intervention is transcatheter aortic balloon valvuloplasty, which relieves the obstruction while avoiding early valve replacement in a growing child; surgery (valvotomy or Ross procedure) is kept for failure or later.
why_wrong_block:
A. Follow up: right for asymptomatic, mild to moderate aortic stenosis with good LV function; this child has symptoms and a significant gradient.
B. Start anticoagulant: plays no role in native valve stenosis in sinus rhythm; anticoagulation is for mechanical valves or atrial fibrillation.
D. Diuretics: may ease congestion in heart failure but do not relieve the fixed outflow obstruction; LV function is good and there is no heart failure here.
key_concept:
Valvular stenosis: symptoms decide intervention; age decides which intervention.
  • Asymptomatic, mild gradient: follow up
  • Symptomatic or significant gradient: intervene
  • Child: balloon valvuloplasty first
  • Adult: surgical or transcatheter valve replacement
  • Critical AS in a neonate: duct dependent, prostaglandin E1 then valvuloplasty
exam_pearl: Same echo in an elderly adult points to valve replacement; in an infant it points to balloon valvuloplasty.

stem: 3y child with persistent expiratory wheezing since urti 2 weeks ago. He has previous history of same complain which resolved using inhaled steroid . There is no history of allergies, eczema. the mother ask you how to deal with it?
OptA: Symptomatic wheezing will disappear by preschool age
OptD: inhaled salbutamol will prevent development of asthma
why_right: Wheezing triggered by a URTI in a 3 year old with no allergies or eczema (no atopy) is episodic viral (transient early) wheeze. Most of these children outgrow it as the airways grow, so the right counselling is reassurance that the symptomatic wheeze is expected to disappear with age (transient early wheeze typically settles by around 6 years). Atopy, a parental asthma history or wheeze between colds would instead raise the risk of persistent asthma.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prolonged antibiotics will worsen symptoms: antibiotics have no role in viral wheeze, so this is not the counselling point; the mother's question is about the course of the wheeze, which is expected to resolve.
C. Corticosteroids will cause diabetes: inhaled corticosteroids at usual doses do not cause diabetes; this is false reassurance in the wrong direction.
D. Inhaled salbutamol will prevent asthma: salbutamol is a reliever that treats bronchospasm; no inhaler, not even an inhaled steroid, changes the natural history or prevents asthma.
key_concept:
Preschool wheeze: viral triggered + no atopy = likely transient.
  • Episodic viral wheeze: only with colds, well between
  • Multiple trigger wheeze: also with exercise, allergens, smoke
  • Persistent asthma risk: eczema, allergies, parental asthma, wheeze between colds
  • Reliever: SABA; controller ICS for frequent or multiple trigger wheeze
  • Diagnosis under 5: history, exam and response to bronchodilator
exam_pearl: Add eczema, food allergy or parental asthma to the stem and the counselling changes to a higher risk of persistent asthma.

stem: 38wk newborn increasing SOB and grunting:
why_right: A term (38 week) newborn with tachypnea and grunting and no mention of meconium-stained liquor most likely has transient tachypnea of the newborn, caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. It is typical after cesarean delivery or near-term birth, shows fluid in the fissures and perihilar streaks on CXR, and usually resolves within a few days with supportive care.
why_wrong_block: A. Meconium aspiration: needs meconium-stained amniotic fluid, usually in a post-term or distressed baby, with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation on CXR; neither is given here.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress by clue:
  • Preterm + ground glass CXR: RDS (surfactant deficiency)
  • Term, cesarean: TTN (fluid in fissures, self limiting)
  • Post-term + meconium liquor: meconium aspiration
  • Maternal GBS, fever, PROM: pneumonia or sepsis
  • Pre vs post ductal saturation gap: PPHN
exam_pearl: TTN improves over 24 to 72 hours; distress that keeps worsening should prompt a search for pneumonia, sepsis or another cause.

stem: Newborn wheezing with chest recession, RR 65 dx:
key_concept:
Noisy breathing in infants: wheeze is lower airway, stridor is upper airway.
  • Coryza then wheeze + crackles, infant: bronchiolitis
  • Barking cough + inspiratory stridor: croup
  • Fever, crackles, sepsis signs, perinatal risk: pneumonia
  • Recurrent wheeze + atopy, older child: asthma
  • Newborn in first hours: think TTN or RDS first
exam_pearl: "Wheeze" rules out croup (stridor) and age rules out asthma; the fork is viral prodrome (bronchiolitis) versus fever or sepsis signs (pneumonia).
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A newborn presents with bleeding from the umbilical stump shortly after it was cut. Laboratory findings are: Platelet count: 18,000/μL PT: normal aPTT: normal The mother has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: mother has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
why_right: Bleeding in a newborn with platelets 18,000 but a normal PT and aPTT means the problem is the platelet count, not the clotting factors. A mother with SLE carries antiplatelet IgG that crosses the placenta and destroys the baby's platelets, so this is an immune (antibody mediated) neonatal thrombocytopenia. This recall's key labels that immune process as neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia, the only immune thrombocytopenia offered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vitamin K deficiency bleeding prolongs the PT (and later aPTT) with a normal platelet count; it fits a home birth with no vitamin K prophylaxis or maternal antiepileptic use, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
C. Hemophilia A gives a prolonged aPTT with normal platelets and normal PT, classically in a boy bleeding after circumcision; here aPTT is normal.
D. A congenital platelet function defect causes bleeding with a normal or only mildly low count (normal in Glanzmann, mildly low with giant platelets in Bernard-Soulier); it does not explain a count of 18,000 or the maternal SLE link.
key_concept:
Neonatal bleeding: read platelets, PT and aPTT together.
  • Low platelets, normal PT/aPTT: immune thrombocytopenia (maternal autoantibody from SLE/ITP, or alloimmune), sepsis, congenital infection
  • Prolonged PT ± aPTT, normal platelets: vitamin K deficiency bleeding
  • Isolated prolonged aPTT: hemophilia A or B
  • Low platelets plus prolonged PT/aPTT and low fibrinogen: DIC
  • Normal count and clotting tests but bleeding: platelet function defect, von Willebrand, factor XIII
exam_pearl: Maternal SLE or ITP in the history plus isolated neonatal thrombocytopenia = antibody transfer from the mother; prolonged PT instead would point to vitamin K.

stem: Child bleeds after umbilical stump His mother has SLE THE child has normal PTt and pt with PLT 18000 what is the TREATMENT?
why_right: The child is actively bleeding (umbilical stump) with platelets 18,000 and normal PT and aPTT, and the mother has SLE, so this is antibody mediated neonatal thrombocytopenia. Platelet transfusion treats the active bleeding immediately, and IVIG blocks the transferred maternal antibodies so platelets survive longer. Together they are the standard management of a bleeding neonate with immune thrombocytopenia.
why_wrong_block:
B. Steroids can be added in immune thrombocytopenia but act slowly and are not first line in a bleeding neonate; they would not stop bleeding now.
C. FFP replaces clotting factors; it is right when PT/aPTT are prolonged (DIC, factor deficiency), but here both are normal.
D. Vitamin K with PCC treats vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which prolongs the PT with normal platelets; here the PT is normal and the platelets are low.
key_concept:
Bleeding neonate: match treatment to the lab pattern.
  • Low platelets, normal PT/aPTT, immune cause: platelets + IVIG
  • Prolonged PT (± aPTT), normal platelets: vitamin K (PCC/FFP if life threatening)
  • Prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, low platelets: DIC, treat cause + FFP/cryo/platelets
  • Older child with post viral ITP and only skin bleeding: often observe; IVIG or steroids if bleeding or very low count
exam_pearl: In an actively bleeding neonate, transfuse platelets even if the cause is immune; IVIG is added to stop ongoing destruction.

stem: What is the cause of TTN?
OptA: delayed clearance or absorption of fetal lung fluid
why_right: Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN) is caused by delayed clearance or absorption of fetal lung fluid. Labour normally triggers the lung epithelium to absorb this fluid, so babies born by elective cesarean section (often at term) are typical. The retained fluid gives mild tachypnea and fluid in the fissures on CXR, and it resolves on its own within days.
why_wrong_block: B. Premature (surfactant deficient) lung causes respiratory distress syndrome in a preterm baby, with a ground glass (reticulogranular) CXR; TTN is typically a term cesarean baby.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress: name the mechanism.
  • TTN: retained fetal lung fluid; term, C-section; perihilar streaks, fluid in fissures; self limiting
  • RDS: surfactant deficiency; preterm; ground glass with air bronchograms
  • Meconium aspiration: post term, meconium stained liquor; patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation
  • Pneumonia: maternal fever, PROM; consolidation
exam_pearl: Term baby + elective C-section + fluid in the horizontal fissure = TTN; preterm + ground glass = RDS.

stem: 12 y/o boy complaining of fever examinations is normal apart from having lymphadenopathy the father said he have history of drinking of unpasteurized milk during farm trip What is most diagnostic?
why_right: Fever with lymphadenopathy after drinking unpasteurized milk on a farm trip points to brucellosis. The recalled option "antibiotic titer" stands for a Brucella antibody titer (serology, e.g. the standard tube agglutination test), which is the diagnostic test used for brucellosis. Blood cultures are slow and often negative, so serology is the practical way to confirm the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. LFTs may be mildly deranged in brucellosis (liver involvement) but are nonspecific and cannot make the diagnosis.
C. CBC may show mild cytopenias or relative lymphocytosis but is nonspecific; it is a supportive test, not a diagnostic one.
D. FNA of a node is invasive and its cytology (e.g. granulomas) is nonspecific; it is right for a persistent localized node, e.g. suspected mycobacterial (M. bovis) lymphadenitis from raw milk or lymphoma, or when serology is negative.
key_concept:
Brucellosis: think raw milk or livestock contact.
  • Gram negative coccobacillus, zoonosis
  • Undulant fever, night sweats, arthralgia, back pain (sacroiliitis), hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
  • Diagnosis: serology (tube agglutination, antibody titer) is the main test
  • Blood or bone marrow culture is definitive but slow and often negative
exam_pearl: Unpasteurized milk in the history = brucellosis; answer the serology (antibody titer), even if the option is oddly worded.

stem: 6 years old Patient with clear case of brucellosis. Hx of Drink raw milk patint had pain in the knee. Which if the following is the first line treatment ?
why_right: Brucellosis (raw milk, joint pain) in a 6 year old: the adult first line regimen is doxycycline based, but tetracyclines are avoided in children under 8 years because of tooth staining and bone effects. The pediatric first line is therefore TMP-SMX plus rifampicin for 6 weeks; a combination is needed because monotherapy relapses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks is first line for adults and children 8 years or older; at 6 years doxycycline is avoided.
C. Ciprofloxacin alone is monotherapy (high relapse rate) and quinolones are not first line in brucellosis, especially in children.
D. Ceftriaxone has poor intracellular activity against Brucella and is not a standard regimen; single agent therapy also relapses.
key_concept:
Brucellosis always needs combination therapy; age and pregnancy pick the partner.
  • Adults and children ≥8 years: doxycycline 6 weeks + rifampicin 6 weeks (or streptomycin for the first 2 to 3 weeks)
  • Children under 8: TMP-SMX + rifampicin for 6 weeks
  • Pregnancy: rifampicin based, avoid doxycycline
  • Spondylitis or sacroiliitis: about 12 weeks
  • Neurobrucellosis: about 6 months
exam_pearl: Same disease, different answer: the child's age under 8 removes doxycycline.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0812).
Compiler note: Age < 8 Years: Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole + Rifampicin for 6 weeks. Age > 8 Years: Doxycycline + Rifampicin for 6 weeks.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with a 2-year history of depression presents to the clinic for followup. Her husband raised a concern about suicide as she is looking more depressed and isolated recently. She denied any history of alcohol or psychoactive substance use. During her clinical exam, there was no eye contact and her systemic exams were unremarkable. Which of the following risk factors carries the highest risk for suicide?
why_right: In a woman with depression who is now more depressed and isolated, social isolation (lack of social support, living alone, withdrawal) is the strongest risk factor among the options. The others either do not apply to her (age 38, female) or are protective (no serious illness).
why_wrong_block:
A. Suicide risk is highest in older patients (and adolescents); 38 is not a high-risk age.
B. Women attempt suicide more often, but men complete suicide more often, so female sex is not the highest-risk factor.
D. Chronic or terminal illness raises suicide risk; its absence is not a risk factor.
key_concept:
Suicide risk factors (SAD PERSONS).
  • Sex male, Age older (or adolescent)
  • Depression, Previous attempt
  • Ethanol/substance use, Rational thinking lost (psychosis)
  • Social support lacking (isolation), Organized plan
  • No spouse, Sickness (chronic illness)
  • Strongest single predictor overall: previous attempt
exam_pearl: Women attempt more, men complete more; among her own features, isolation is the danger sign.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with recent history of feeling tiredness, fatigue and weight loss. She noticed as well worsening of her chronic constipation. Stool for occult blood was positive (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values RBC 3 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) 4.2-5.4 x 1012/L (Female) Hb 89 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) HCT 0.25 0.42-0.52 (Male) 0.37-0.48 (Female) Platelets count 234 150-400 × 109/L Which of the following is the best next step in diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Stool for occult blood was positive
why_right: A "60-year-old" with fatigue, weight loss, worsening constipation (change in bowel habit), anemia (Hb 89) and a positive stool occult blood test has colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. Colonoscopy is the best next step because it visualizes the entire colon and allows biopsy and removal of polyps in the same session.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT enterography images the small bowel (Crohn disease, obscure small bowel bleeding) and cannot take tissue; it is not the test for a suspected colon cancer.
B. Barium enema is outdated, misses small lesions and cannot biopsy; it is used only when colonoscopy is impossible.
C. Sigmoidoscopy sees only the distal colon and would miss a right-sided cancer, which typically causes anemia; a positive occult blood test needs full colonoscopy.
key_concept:
Positive FOBT/FIT or iron deficiency anemia with red flags = colonoscopy.
  • Colonoscopy: whole colon + biopsy + polypectomy
  • Sigmoid cancer found on sigmoidoscopy: still need full colonoscopy for synchronous lesions
  • After diagnosis: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
  • Barium enema or CT colonography: only if colonoscopy not possible
exam_pearl: Never repeat a positive occult blood test or settle for a partial exam; go to colonoscopy.

stem: Patient presented with weight loss (and other dyspepsia Symptoms) Gastric antrum Histopathology confirmed Adenocarcinoma. How to stage the “T”?
why_right: The lead-in asks specifically how to stage the "T", which is the depth of tumour invasion through the gastric wall layers. Endoscopic ultrasound resolves the individual wall layers and nearby nodes, so it is the most accurate test for T (and local N) staging of gastric cancer. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is still done first overall to look for distant metastases (M).
why_wrong_block:
B. Transabdominal ultrasound cannot resolve the layers of the stomach wall; at most it may show liver metastases or ascites.
C. A nuclear (bone) scan looks for skeletal metastases when symptoms suggest them; it says nothing about depth of invasion.
D. A contrast (Gastrografin) study outlines the lumen and mucosa or shows a leak, but cannot measure how deep the tumour penetrates the wall.
key_concept:
TNM staging tools for upper GI cancer.
  • Diagnosis: upper endoscopy with biopsy
  • M (distant spread): CT chest, abdomen and pelvis first
  • T and local N: endoscopic ultrasound
  • Occult peritoneal disease: staging laparoscopy
  • PET-CT: occult distant metastases (more in esophageal cancer)
exam_pearl: "Next investigation after biopsy" = CT CAP; "how to assess T / depth of invasion" = EUS.

stem: A 62-year-old man has been noticing progressive difficulty swallowing, first solid food and now liquids as well. A barium study shows a ragged narrowing just below the carinal level. Endoscopic biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following provides the most accurate information regarding the T stage of an esophageal carcinoma?
highlight_terms_source: T stage of an esophageal carcinoma
why_right: The lead-in asks for "the most accurate information regarding the T stage", which is depth of invasion through the esophageal wall. Endoscopic ultrasound visualizes each wall layer and periesophageal nodes, making it the most accurate test for T (and local N) staging of esophageal cancer once biopsy has confirmed the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT is the first staging scan for distant metastases and gross invasion of neighbouring organs, but it cannot separate the wall layers to define early T stage.
B. PET is best for detecting occult distant metastases (M stage); its spatial resolution is too low to judge depth of wall invasion.
C. MRI is not a routine staging tool for esophageal cancer and is less accurate than EUS for wall depth.
E. Bronchoscopy checks for tracheobronchial invasion in tumours at or above the carina; it shows airway involvement, not the tumour's depth in the esophageal wall.
key_concept:
Esophageal cancer workup: biopsy, then stage in layers.
  • Diagnosis: endoscopy with biopsy (barium shows a ragged stricture)
  • Distant spread: CT chest and abdomen, then PET-CT
  • T and local N: endoscopic ultrasound
  • Upper or mid tumour near the airway: bronchoscopy for tracheal invasion
  • SCC: upper/mid esophagus, smoking, alcohol, achalasia; adenocarcinoma: lower, Barrett, GERD
exam_pearl: T = EUS, M = CT/PET; bronchoscopy only answers "is the airway invaded".

stem: A child exhibits scissoring of the legs when held upright. MRI reveals periventricular leukomalacia. Which of the following is most strongly support the diagnosis?
OptD: Periventricular white matter changes on MRI
why_right: Scissoring of the legs plus periventricular leukomalacia describes spastic diplegic cerebral palsy. CP is a clinical diagnosis, and diplegia is defined by its examination finding: bilateral lower limb spasticity, with the legs more affected than the arms. Periventricular white matter injury damages the leg fibres that run closest to the ventricles, which is why the legs bear the brunt.
why_wrong_block:
A. Static (non progressive) motor delay is common to every CP type and also to other static brain injuries; it supports CP in general but does not define the diplegic pattern seen here.
C. Prematurity is a risk factor for periventricular leukomalacia and diplegia, not a finding that establishes the diagnosis; many preterm babies never develop CP.
D. Periventricular white matter changes are the cause already given in the stem; imaging supports the etiology, but the CP subtype is diagnosed from the clinical tone pattern.
key_concept:
CP types by limb pattern.
  • Spastic diplegia: legs more than arms, scissoring; prematurity, periventricular leukomalacia
  • Spastic hemiplegia: one side, arm more than leg; perinatal stroke
  • Spastic quadriplegia: all four limbs severely; severe hypoxic ischemic injury
  • Dyskinetic: involuntary movements; basal ganglia injury (kernicterus, acute asphyxia)
  • CP is non progressive; a progressive picture suggests another disorder
exam_pearl: Scissoring + preterm + periventricular leukomalacia = spastic diplegia; the diagnosis rests on the bilateral leg spasticity, not on the MRI.

stem: A 10 YO child with URTI 2 weeks ago brought by mother concerned because his uncle has leukemia and his brother has retinoblastoma. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: The relevant family history is the brother with retinoblastoma: it can be heritable (germline RB1 mutation), so siblings need eye examination by an ophthalmologist to assess for retinoblastoma. The recent URTI and the uncle's leukemia do not call for investigation in a well child.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC would be right if the child had symptoms of leukemia (pallor, bruising, bone pain, fever, hepatosplenomegaly); an uncle with leukemia is not an indication in a well child.
B. CXR has no role here; it would be for a suspected chest infection or a mediastinal mass (e.g. T cell leukemia/lymphoma), and a self limiting URTI 2 weeks ago in a well child needs no imaging.
D. BRCA 1/2 testing is for families with breast, ovarian, prostate or pancreatic cancer; it is unrelated to retinoblastoma or leukemia.
key_concept:
Retinoblastoma in a sibling = ophthalmology screening.
  • Heritable form: germline RB1 mutation, often bilateral and early
  • Siblings and offspring: dilated eye examination by ophthalmology, plus genetic counselling and RB1 testing
  • Heritable RB1 carriers also have a later risk of second cancers (e.g. osteosarcoma)
  • Leukocoria at any age: urgent ophthalmology referral
exam_pearl: Work out which relative's cancer is heritable and relevant: retinoblastoma in a first degree relative drives the referral, not the uncle's leukemia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed 964 block has no highlight; the compiler's fuller 'Q:' restatement (next page) highlights 'refer to ophtha to assess for Retinoblastoma' (options there: A CXR to exclude Leukemia, B BRCA 1&2, C CBC to exclude anemia, D refer to ophtha).

stem: Case Of Post-Operative Fever - 4 days post abdominal surgery, pale, hypotensive with cold extremities. how to confirm iV fluid level in patient who is being treated for dehydration?
why_right: This recall's key is CVP 8 because the question asks how to confirm the "IV fluid level" (intravascular filling) in a hypovolemic patient, and CVP is the classic direct estimate of right-sided filling pressure. A CVP of 8 sits in the traditional resuscitation target range of 8 to 12 mmHg, whereas each of the other values is either clearly abnormal or a perfusion marker rather than a volume measure.
why_wrong_block:
B. A MAP of 45 is profound hypotension; the usual resuscitation target is a MAP of at least 65, so this value shows ongoing shock, not adequate fluid.
C. Urine output of 0.1 mL/kg/h is severe oliguria; adequate resuscitation is shown by at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults.
D. Lactate reflects tissue perfusion and anaerobic metabolism rather than intravascular volume, and a value of 2 sits at the upper limit of normal, so on this key's logic it does not confirm fluid status.
key_concept:
Resuscitation endpoints: know the target for each number.
  • CVP: traditional target 8 to 12 mmHg (static, limited predictor)
  • MAP: at least 65 mmHg
  • Urine output: at least 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, at least 1 mL/kg/h children
  • Lactate: normal up to 2 mmol/L; falling lactate = improving perfusion
  • Burns: urine output is the main endpoint
exam_pearl: The same four options appear in a burn recall keyed to lactate 2; read whether the question asks for "fluid level" (CVP here) or "good resuscitation".

stem: Patient came to ER with burns all over the body after intubation and resuscitation what will indicate good fluid…
why_right: After intubation and resuscitation of extensive burns, the question asks which value indicates "good fluid" resuscitation. Urine output is the usual burn endpoint, but here it is only 0.1 mL/kg/h, so the remaining sign of adequate tissue perfusion is a lactate of 2, which is at the upper limit of normal and shows no significant anaerobic metabolism. CVP is unreliable in burns and MAP 45 is shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine output is the best burn endpoint, but the target is at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (1 mL/kg/h in children); 0.1 mL/kg/h means under-resuscitation.
B. A MAP of 45 is severe hypotension and indicates inadequate resuscitation; the target is a MAP of at least 65.
C. CVP is invasive and a poor predictor of volume status in burns, where massive capillary leak and fluid shifts distort it; it is not used as the resuscitation endpoint.
key_concept:
Burn resuscitation: titrate fluids to perfusion endpoints.
  • Main endpoint: urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, 1 mL/kg/h children
  • Supporting: normal or falling lactate
  • Heart rate and BP: unreliable (pain, catecholamines)
  • CVP: poor predictor, not a target
  • Fluid: Ringer lactate by Parkland formula, then adjust to urine output
exam_pearl: If the urine output option is below target, pick the next perfusion marker that is normal (lactate), not CVP.

stem: 10 years old girl came to the ER complaining from RLQ abdominal pain that associated with nausea and 3 times vomiting, there is pain and rebound tenderness in examination. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A school-age child with RLQ pain, nausea and vomiting, and rebound tenderness on examination has the classic picture of acute appendicitis. Rebound tenderness signals localized peritoneal irritation in the right iliac fossa, which fits an inflamed appendix. In a child, ultrasound is the first imaging if confirmation is needed, followed by appendectomy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intussusception: typically an infant or toddler (about 6 months to 3 years) with episodic colicky crying, drawing up the legs, a sausage-shaped mass and red currant jelly stool; a 10-year-old with localized RLQ peritonism does not fit.
C. Meckel's diverticulum: classically presents in young children with painless rectal bleeding; Meckel's diverticulitis can mimic appendicitis but is far rarer, so it is not the diagnosis for this classic picture.
key_concept:
RLQ pain + nausea/vomiting + rebound tenderness = acute appendicitis until proven otherwise.
  • Pain often starts periumbilical, then migrates to the RLQ
  • Anorexia, low-grade fever, McBurney point tenderness, Rovsing sign
  • Imaging: US in children and pregnancy; CT best in non-pregnant adults
  • Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
exam_pearl: Age flips the answer: infant with colicky pain and a mass = intussusception; toddler with painless bleeding = Meckel's; school-age child with RLQ peritonism = appendicitis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A 'Q:' variant: 14 years old female with periumbilical pain shifting to the right, anorexia, mild diarrhea + dysuria, no vomiting/fever, right tenderness increasing with cough; options Appendicitis / Gastroenteritis / Right ureteric stone / UTI; highlighted A) Appendicitis.

stem: 4 years old starting experiencing bone pain, fever, and something for 3 weeks. Examination: abdominal hepatosplenomegaly only Labs: platelet 70 WBC 30 Hgb low ( between 8-11 ? ) Nothing else is given What is the indicated diagnostic test?
why_right: A 4 year old with bone pain, fever and hepatosplenomegaly, plus a high WBC (30), low platelets (70) and anemia, has leukemia (most likely ALL) until proven otherwise. Bone pain reflects marrow infiltration and the cytopenias reflect marrow failure. The test that establishes the diagnosis is examination of the bone marrow (aspirate and biopsy).
why_wrong_block: A. EBV PCR or serology suits infectious mononucleosis (fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes), which does not cause bone pain with anemia and marked thrombocytopenia.
key_concept:
Child with cytopenias + bone pain = marrow problem.
  • Leukemia features: fever, pallor, bruising/petechiae, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
  • WBC may be high, normal or low; blasts on smear are a clue
  • First: CBC and peripheral smear
  • Diagnostic: bone marrow aspirate/biopsy (with immunophenotyping)
exam_pearl: Bone pain with two or more cytopenias in a child = leukemia; confirm in the marrow, not with viral serology.

stem: 2 years old boy was playing with his brother and fell downstairs had brief jircky movements at home and on exam was drwosy and lathergic What is the most appropriate ( without next)
why_right: After a fall downstairs this child had brief jerky movements (a post traumatic seizure) and is now drowsy and lethargic, which is altered mental status. Under the pediatric head injury (PECARN) rules, altered mental status is a high risk criterion that mandates an urgent non contrast CT brain to look for intracranial bleeding. The lead in asks for the most appropriate action, and imaging must come before deciding on surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation is acceptable only with normal mental status and exam, as in a child who vomited or had a headache but is fully alert; drowsiness after a seizure removes that option.
C. Electrolytes are for an unprovoked or febrile seizure without trauma; here the trigger is head injury, so intracranial injury must be excluded first.
D. Neurosurgery referral follows a CT showing a surgical lesion such as an epidural or subdural hematoma; without imaging there is nothing to refer yet.
key_concept:
PECARN pediatric head trauma:
  • High risk (CT now): GCS below 15, altered mental status, palpable or basilar skull fracture signs
  • Intermediate (observe vs CT): LOC, vomiting, severe headache, severe mechanism
  • Low risk: observe, no CT
  • Seizure plus drowsiness after trauma = CT brain
exam_pearl: Alert child who vomited = observe; drowsy child after a seizure = CT brain.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2366).
Compiler note: ✅ CT brain without contrast. Observation is only for low-risk patients with normal mental status. Blood electrolytes not correct: seizure here is trauma-related, not metabolic. Neurosurgery referral comes after imaging if CT shows pathology.

stem: A 6 weeks child present with absent red reflex in left eye (leukocoria), he is developing normally. What is the diagnosis?
key_concept:
Leukocoria: retinoblastoma or cataract until proven otherwise.
  • Retinoblastoma: under 5 years, leukocoria then strabismus, may be heritable
  • Congenital cataract: present at birth, rubella, galactosemia, inherited
  • Toxocariasis: older child, dog/soil exposure, unilateral
  • Management of any leukocoria: urgent ophthalmology referral for a dilated eye examination
exam_pearl: If the stem says 'tumor' or gives a family history, answer retinoblastoma; if it gives congenital infection or galactosemia clues, answer cataract.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler note: 'B/C???' (unresolved).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: boy with bacterial sinusitis , started on amoxicillin, didn’t improve after 3 days , what to do ?
why_right: Acute bacterial sinusitis treated with amoxicillin that has not improved after 3 days (72 h) is treatment failure, most likely from a beta lactamase producing organism (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) or resistant pneumococcus. The next step is to switch to amoxicillin clavulanate (high dose) without imaging, as long as there are no complication signs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance and continuing the same drug is wrong once there is no improvement at 72 h; that defines failure of first line therapy.
B. ENT referral is for complications (orbital or intracranial), recurrent or chronic sinusitis, or failure of second line antibiotics; a single amoxicillin failure is handled by broadening the antibiotic.
key_concept:
Pediatric acute bacterial sinusitis ladder.
  • First line: amoxicillin (with or without clavulanate)
  • Worse or no better at 72 h: amoxicillin clavulanate, high dose
  • Penicillin allergy: options include a third generation cephalosporin or clindamycin based regimens
  • Failure of second line or complication signs: contrast CT and specialist referral
exam_pearl: No improvement at 72 h means change the antibiotic, not image; eye or neuro signs mean CT.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: fever, stuffed nose, headaches, bacterial sinusitis with no improvement after 72 hrs of amoxicillin; options A Refer to ENT, B CT Sinuses, C change medication to Amoxicillin clavulanate for 10 days, D change diagnosis; Answer: C.

stem: 90 year old male living in residential community comes complaining of severe abdominal pain in the last 24 hours. The abdomen was soft and lax, tender all over, hyperactive abdominal sounds. (no rigidity) What is the next step:
highlight_terms_source: soft and lax, tender all over
why_right: A 90-year-old from a residential (care) home with diffuse tenderness, a soft, lax abdomen with no rigidity and hyperactive bowel sounds needs a complete bedside examination before any test, and that includes a digital rectal examination. In frail, immobile elderly patients DRE quickly detects fecal impaction (a common cause of pain and obstructive symptoms), rectal masses and blood (hinting at ischemia or malignancy). It is cheap, immediate and guides the choice of further investigation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy: an elective, preparation-requiring investigation, not the next step in acute severe abdominal pain; it is used for bleeding or suspected colorectal cancer once the acute picture is clarified.
B. Sigmoidoscopy: useful for suspected sigmoid volvulus (huge tympanic distension, coffee bean sign) or distal lesions, but should follow examination, not replace it.
C. US abdomen: reasonable imaging for biliary or pelvic causes, but the bedside examination (including DRE) is completed first; in a frail elderly patient with diffuse pain, CT is usually the more informative imaging.
key_concept:
Acute abdomen in the elderly: complete the examination (including DRE) before imaging.
  • Nursing home + immobility: think fecal impaction
  • DRE: impaction, rectal mass, blood on the glove
  • Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen: think mesenteric ischemia (CT angiography)
  • Massive tympanic distension + coffee bean sign: sigmoid volvulus (sigmoidoscopic decompression)
exam_pearl: Soft, non-rigid abdomen in an elderly patient does not exclude serious pathology; the elderly often lack peritoneal signs.

stem: A 2month old baby(chronological age) born at 34weeks gestation. Mother present to the clinic for immunization.
why_right: A baby born at "34 weeks" who is now "2 month old (chronological age)" gets the routine 2-month vaccines today. Preterm infants are immunized at the same chronological age as term infants, with full doses; prematurity does not delay or reduce vaccination.
why_wrong_block:
B. There is no separate "prematurity" schedule; corrected age is used for growth and developmental assessment, not for vaccine timing.
C. Waiting until 6 months leaves a vulnerable preterm infant unprotected; the only common timing nuance is the hepatitis B birth dose in very low birth weight babies.
key_concept:
Preterm infants: vaccinate by chronological age, full dose.
  • Vaccines: chronological age, usual schedule, usual dose
  • Growth and development: corrected age
  • No dose reduction, no delay for prematurity
exam_pearl: Corrected age is for milestones, never for vaccines.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall (2 months old, premature at 34 weeks, how to give vaccine; A wait till 6 months, B follow his chronological age) highlights 'follow his chronological age'; screenshot: 'Right is: A. Immunize according to chronological age'. Concordant.

stem: 32 years old male admitted for motor vehicle accident, after initially stabilization and multiple surgical interventions for fractures. He is in pos-op care Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measures?
why_right: After major trauma and multiple fracture surgeries, the main preventable complications are those of immobility: DVT/PE, pneumonia and atelectasis, pressure ulcers, muscle wasting and joint stiffness. Early mobilization and physiotherapy address all of these, which is why it is the most appropriate preventive measure in the post-operative phase (alongside pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis when bleeding risk allows).
why_wrong_block:
A. Extended bed rest: increases the risk of DVT/PE, pneumonia, pressure sores and deconditioning; it is the opposite of prevention.
B. High-dose corticosteroids: no preventive role after trauma surgery; they impair wound and fracture healing and raise infection risk.
D. Empirical antibiotics for 5 days: surgical prophylaxis is short (a single pre-incision dose, at most about 24 h for closed fractures); prolonged empirical courses promote resistance and C. difficile without benefit.
key_concept:
Post-operative prevention after polytrauma = fight immobility.
  • Early mobilization and physiotherapy
  • VTE prophylaxis: LMWH when bleeding risk allows, mechanical devices otherwise
  • Incentive spirometry / chest physiotherapy against atelectasis and pneumonia
  • Pressure area care
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: short, peri-incisional only
exam_pearl: Bed rest is never the preventive answer post-op; mobilization is.

stem: A mother brings her daughter for a pre-school follow-up visit. She is concerned because her daughter has shown decreased physical activity, gets easily fatigued during outdoor play, and spends a lot of time watching TV. The child’s weight is within the expected range, and there are no other concerning symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to improve her energy and activity levels?
OptA: Give multivitamin supplements to increase energy
OptD: Encourage increased physical activity and limit screen time
highlight_terms_source: spends a lot of time watching TV
weight is within the expected range
why_right: The child has low activity, tires during outdoor play and "spends a lot of time watching TV", but her "weight is within the expected range" and there are "no other concerning symptoms". This is a lifestyle problem (deconditioning from sedentary screen time), so the fix is more physical activity and limiting screen time.
why_wrong_block:
A. Multivitamins do not raise energy in a well-nourished child with normal growth; they fit a documented deficiency or restricted diet.
B. Her weight is normal, so extra calories would only promote overweight in a sedentary child; they fit undernutrition or faltering growth.
C. Endocrine referral needs red flags (growth failure, abnormal weight, goitre, other symptoms of hypothyroidism); none are present.
key_concept:
Well child, normal growth, sedentary: counsel lifestyle first.
  • Encourage daily active play
  • Limit recreational screen time
  • Investigate or refer only with red flags: weight loss, faltering growth, pallor, other systemic symptoms
exam_pearl: Normal weight and no other symptoms rule out the supplement, calorie and referral options.

stem: A 25-year-old patient sustained a blunt trauma to the right chest wall; there was paradoxical movement of the right side of the chest (see report). Heart rate 96 /min Respiratory rate 35 /min Oxygen saturation 84 % Chest X-ray: Fracture 2nd through 4th ribs at more than 1 site. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: Fracture 2nd through 4th ribs at more than 1 site
why_right: Ribs 2 to 4 fractured at more than one site with paradoxical chest movement is flail chest. The danger is hypoxia from the unstable segment and the underlying pulmonary contusion, here shown by SpO2 84% and RR 35. Initial management is supportive: adequate analgesia plus oxygenation and assisted ventilation, with intubation when hypoxia persists (SpO2 below about 88% is a trauma intubation trigger).
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluid resuscitation: the patient is not hypotensive (HR 96, no shock); the problem is respiratory, and excess fluid worsens pulmonary contusion. Fluids would lead if he were in hemorrhagic shock.
C. Needle decompression: treats tension pneumothorax (hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension), none of which is described.
D. Thoracostomy chest tube: for pneumothorax or hemothorax seen on examination or X-ray; the film here shows only rib fractures.
key_concept:
Flail chest = 2 or more adjacent ribs fractured in 2 or more places + paradoxical movement.
  • Problem: hypoxia from the flail segment and pulmonary contusion
  • Treatment: analgesia (including regional blocks), oxygen, assisted ventilation
  • Intubate if hypoxia persists or respiratory failure develops
  • Avoid fluid overload (contusion worsens)
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
exam_pearl: Paradoxical movement means flail chest (ventilate and give analgesia); hyperresonance with tracheal shift means tension pneumothorax (decompress).
compiler_note: Compiler note: A second version (option B 'Assistant ventilation') also gives 'Answer: B'.

stem: A Child brought by his mother with lethargy, pallor, low grade subjective fever, lymphadenopathy for 2 months, What’s initial to Confirm diagnosis?
why_right: "Lethargy, pallor", fever and "lymphadenopathy for 2 months" with low Hb and low platelets (two cell lines down) is leukemia until proven otherwise. The lead-in asks what will "confirm" the diagnosis, and only bone marrow examination does that, by showing blast infiltration and allowing typing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood film is the first screening test and may show blasts, but it cannot confirm leukemia (blasts can be absent in the periphery, especially with a normal WBC). It would be the answer only if the lead-in asked for the first screening test; here "initial" is tied to "confirm".
B. Virology (EBV, CMV) fits an infectious mononucleosis-like picture with tender nodes and short illness; 2 months of nodes plus bicytopenia needs marrow examination.
key_concept:
Suspected childhood leukemia: blood film screens, bone marrow confirms.
  • Red flags: persistent pallor, fever, bruising, bone pain, non-tender nodes, hepatosplenomegaly
  • Cytopenias with a normal WBC do not exclude leukemia
  • CBC + film: first step
  • Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy: diagnostic
exam_pearl: "Confirm" means bone marrow; "first test" alone would mean CBC and film.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot note from recaller: low Hb and low plt but WBC normal; the q is about initial to confirm the dx.

stem: Case of retinoblastoma 2 year child with absent red reflective. How to diagnose and stage?
why_right: In a 2-year-old with retinoblastoma ("absent red reflex"), imaging is needed to stage the tumour: optic nerve extension, orbital spread and associated pineal tumour. MRI of the brain and orbits does this best and involves no radiation, which matters because heritable RB1 carriers are prone to radiation-induced second cancers.
why_wrong_block: A. CT is avoided in retinoblastoma because radiation increases second malignancy risk in RB1 carriers, and it shows soft-tissue and optic nerve extension less well; CT is the first choice in stroke or trauma, not here.
key_concept:
Leukocoria pathway: examine first, then MRI to stage.
  • Absent red reflex: urgent ophthalmology, dilated fundoscopy under anesthesia
  • Ocular ultrasound supports the diagnosis
  • Staging: MRI brain and orbits (optic nerve, pineal gland)
  • Avoid CT: radiation and second tumours (e.g. osteosarcoma)
exam_pearl: Retinoblastoma + imaging choice = MRI; CT is the trap because of radiation risk.

stem: Man 6 months after bariatric surgery successfully losing weight and adherent to his diet and exercise but he is worried about long term success, he is at which of the following stages?
highlight_terms_source: adherent to his diet and exercise
why_right: The transtheoretical (stages of change) model labels a person who has sustained the new behaviour for about 6 months or longer as being in maintenance. He is "6 months after" surgery, is "successfully losing weight" and "adherent" to diet and exercise, and his concern is now "long term success", which is exactly the task of maintenance: preventing relapse. So the key is maintenance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Action: the first months (under about 6) of actively doing the new behaviour. He has passed that window and is now focused on keeping the change, not starting it.
C. Contemplation: aware of the problem and thinking about changing within the next months but not yet acting. He is already acting consistently.
D. Pre-contemplation: no intention to change and often denies the problem. He has had surgery and changed his lifestyle, so this clearly does not fit.
key_concept:
Stages of change: identify where the patient is by intention and by how long the change has lasted.
  • Pre-contemplation: no intention to change
  • Contemplation: considering change, ambivalent
  • Preparation: planning, small steps, change imminent
  • Action: actively changing, under about 6 months
  • Maintenance: change sustained about 6 months or more, focus on relapse prevention
  • Relapse: return to old behaviour, can re-enter the cycle
exam_pearl: The 6 month mark separates action from maintenance; worry about keeping the change long term points to maintenance.

stem: Pelvic fracture with BP 88/55. Next step?
why_right: A pelvic fracture with BP 88/55 means hemorrhagic shock from pelvic bleeding, which can be massive. Current trauma resuscitation favors early blood products (balanced transfusion) over large-volume crystalloid in a hypotensive bleeding trauma patient, together with a pelvic binder and definitive hemorrhage control (angioembolization or preperitoneal packing). The key here is therefore blood transfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bed rest: appropriate only for a stable, minor (e.g. pubic ramus) fracture; useless in a hypotensive patient.
B. Laparotomy: pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal and is not controlled by laparotomy; laparotomy is for intra-abdominal bleeding with a positive FAST in an unstable patient.
C. IV fluids: a limited initial crystalloid bolus may be given while blood is prepared, but large-volume crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens bleeding; ongoing shock from pelvic hemorrhage needs blood.
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture = hemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise.
  • Pelvic binder to close the pelvic volume
  • Early blood products (massive transfusion protocol if needed)
  • Limit crystalloid
  • Hemorrhage control: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing / external fixation
  • Positive FAST + unstable: laparotomy for the abdomen, not the pelvis
exam_pearl: If 'pelvic binder' appears among the options, it usually comes first; otherwise blood beats crystalloid in hemorrhagic shock.

stem: Pediatric patient came with dull headache that wakes him from sleep, has photosensitivity. Asking which of the following indication for neuroimaging?
why_right: A headache that "wakes him from sleep" is a classic red flag for raised intracranial pressure (e.g. a posterior fossa tumour), because pressure rises when lying flat at night. That makes it the indication for neuroimaging, while the other features fit a primary headache such as migraine.
why_wrong_block:
A. Poor response to analgesics is common in migraine and medication-overuse headache; on its own it is not an imaging indication.
B. Photosensitivity is a typical migraine feature (with phonophobia and nausea) and does not suggest a structural lesion.
D. Vomiting with headache attacks is common in migraine; it becomes a red flag only when it is early-morning or persistent vomiting with a worsening pattern.
key_concept:
Pediatric headache: image only with red flags.
  • Wakes the child from sleep, or worst on waking in the morning
  • Early-morning vomiting
  • Progressive worsening or change in pattern
  • Abnormal neurological exam, papilledema, ataxia, head tilt
  • Young age (under about 3 to 6 years), growth or behaviour change
  • Migraine features (photophobia, nausea, family history): no imaging
exam_pearl: Plain vomiting fits migraine; morning vomiting with a sleep-waking headache means imaging.

stem: 4 months old infant is brought to the clinic due to cyanosis during crying and poor weight gain. and growth is below the 3rd centile admitted as case of Tracheomalacia. What is the next best step in management?
why_right: Most tracheomalacia is mild and resolves by 1 to 2 years, but this infant has severe disease: "cyanosis during crying" (airway collapse) and "poor weight gain" with growth "below the 3rd centile". Severe tracheomalacia with cyanotic episodes or failure to thrive needs referral for surgical evaluation (e.g. aortopexy, tracheostomy or stenting).
why_wrong_block:
A. Inhaled corticosteroids treat airway inflammation (asthma); tracheomalacia is a structural softening of cartilage and steroids do not stiffen it.
B. Home oxygen may support hypoxia but does not prevent the dynamic collapse or fix the failure to thrive; it fits stable chronic hypoxia, not severe malacia.
D. Beta-2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle and can make a floppy trachea collapse more; they are for bronchospasm, not malacia.
key_concept:
Tracheomalacia: severity decides observation vs surgery.
  • Mild (noisy breathing, normal growth): reassure, self-limiting by 1 to 2 years
  • Diagnosis: bronchoscopy
  • Severe (cyanotic spells, recurrent pneumonia, failure to thrive): surgical referral
  • Bronchodilators can worsen malacia
exam_pearl: Normal growth means wait; cyanosis plus growth below the 3rd centile means surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another recall of the same question in this block: 'infant with tracheomalachia present with grunting and cyanosis: Rx?' A. Systemic steroid, B. Home oxygen, C. Refer to surgery, D. Albuterol (no answer marked).

stem: patient with tracheomalacia presents with recurrent pneumonia and failure to thrive. What management?
why_right: Tracheomalacia is usually self-limiting, but "recurrent pneumonia" (poor clearance of secretions through a collapsing airway) and "failure to thrive" mark severe disease. Severe, complicated tracheomalacia is an indication for surgical correction rather than waiting for spontaneous resolution.
why_wrong_block: A. Conservative observation is right for mild tracheomalacia with noisy breathing and normal growth; complications like recurrent pneumonia and failure to thrive mean waiting is no longer safe.
key_concept:
Tracheomalacia indications for surgery: complications, not the diagnosis itself.
  • Recurrent pneumonia
  • Failure to thrive
  • Cyanotic or apneic spells
  • Failure to extubate or ventilator dependence
  • Otherwise: observe, resolves by 1 to 2 years
exam_pearl: Same disease, two answers: uncomplicated = observe, complicated = surgery.

stem: A 4 months old baby presents with monophasic expiratory wheeze. He is at the 50th percentile for weight and normal height. There is no respiratory distress. These features suggest tracheomalacia. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: 50th percentile for weight and normal height
why_right: The stem names the diagnosis ("features suggest tracheomalacia") and every clue is benign: a "monophasic expiratory wheeze" from a floppy central airway, normal growth ("50th percentile") and "no respiratory distress". Tracheomalacia is self limiting and the airway firms up as the cartilage matures, usually by 1 to 2 years. So the most appropriate management is to reassure the parents and follow up.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nebulized SABA: the wheeze is from dynamic collapse of a soft trachea, not bronchospasm, so bronchodilators do not help (they can even worsen collapse by relaxing airway smooth muscle). Right for asthma or reactive airway wheeze, which is polyphonic and responds to bronchodilators.
B. Systemic steroids: there is no airway inflammation to treat. Right for an acute asthma exacerbation or croup, not a structural floppy airway.
D. Tracheostomy: reserved for severe tracheomalacia with life threatening apnoeic spells, recurrent respiratory failure or failure to thrive. This infant is thriving with no distress.
key_concept:
Mild tracheo/laryngomalacia in a thriving infant = reassure and observe.
  • Both: noisy breathing, cough, wheeze or stridor in early infancy
  • Tracheomalacia: monophasic expiratory wheeze; diagnosis by bronchoscopy
  • Laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor, worse supine, better prone; diagnosis by laryngoscopy
  • Natural history: resolves by 1 to 2 years
  • Intervene only for red flags: failure to thrive, apnoea, cyanosis, severe distress
exam_pearl: Monophasic (single pitch) central wheeze = floppy airway, polyphonic wheeze = asthma; add failure to thrive or apnoea and the answer moves from reassurance to intervention.
